title: hugo mod npm pack emits a publishable, checkout-named package.json
body:
**TL;DR**: the generated `package.json` has no `"private": true` and a checkout-derived `name`, so committed copies are publishable under names sites don't control. Suggested fix: emit `"private": true` and a stable (ideally scoped) default name.

### What version of Hugo are you using (`hugo version`)?

```
hugo v0.165.0-76a5e1880ab46688155b02e99bab9be2a6134492+extended darwin/arm64 BuildDate=2026-08-12T14:26:28Z VendorInfo=gohugoio
```

### Does this issue reproduce with the latest release?

Yes (transcript below is v0.165.0). The behavior is in master's [package_builder.go](https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/blob/master/modules/npm/package_builder.go).

### What happened

`hugo mod npm pack` writes `packages/hugoautogen/package.json` with:

- a **name derived from the checkout directory**, so it varies per clone and can be a registry name the site doesn't control, and
- **no `"private": true`**, npm's do-not-publish guard for internal packages.

The file is regenerated wholesale on each run, so hand-set fields don't survive. From a fresh clone of a repo whose committed copy was hand-normalized:

```console
$ git clone https://github.com/google/docsy-example.git site-a && cd site-a
$ grep -E '"(name|version|private)"' packages/hugoautogen/package.json
  "name": "@docsy/hugoautogen",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "private": true
$ hugo mod npm pack
$ grep -E '"(name|version|private)"' packages/hugoautogen/package.json
  "name": "site-a",
  "version": "0.1.0"
```

A sibling clone of the same repo into `site-b` yields `"name": "site-b"`.

### Why it matters

Sites that commit the generated workspace (e.g. so `npm ci` works without running Hugo first) end up carrying a manifest that npm workspace publishing and common release tools treat as publishable by default: `npm publish --dry-run --workspaces` packs it as `site-a@0.1.0`, while with `"private": true` npm skips the workspace. The name variance also churns the committed manifest, and the lockfile's workspace entry, across differently named checkouts.

### What did you expect

The generated internal workspace is non-publishable (`"private": true`) and has a stable, project-controlled default name rather than the checkout directory's basename. Ideally the default is scoped: a bare name can be claimed on the registry by anyone, a scoped one only by the scope owner.

### Workaround

[docsy-example#487](https://github.com/google/docsy-example/pull/487) follows each pack invocation with a single `npm pkg set` line restoring a scoped name and `private`.

Happy to send a PR for the `private` field (and for the name default, if you have a preference for what it should be).

title: GetSortedMapValues reads the map after releasing the read lock, so a concurrent SetInMap aborts the build
body:
### What version of Hugo are you using (`hugo version`)? 
$ hugo version
hugo v0.164.0-ce2470e7012b5ab5fc4e10ebe4027e9f8d9e00dc+extended windows/amd64 BuildDate=2026-07-06T16:39:30Z VendorInfo=gohugoio
### Does this issue reproduce with the latest release? Yes. `common/hstore/scratch.go` is byte-identical at `v0.164.0`, at `v0.165.0` and on `master`, and the line numbers cited below are the same in all three. --- `Scratch.GetSortedMapValues` holds the read lock only long enough to fetch the map header out of `c.values`. It releases the lock and then iterates and indexes that map: ```go // common/hstore/scratch.go @ v0.165.0 func (c *Scratch) GetSortedMapValues(key string) any { c.mu.RLock() if c.values[key] == nil { c.mu.RUnlock() return nil } unsortedMap := c.values[key].(map[string]any) c.mu.RUnlock() // L141: lock released here var keys []string for mapKey := range unsortedMap { // L143: map iteration, unlocked keys = append(keys, mapKey) } sort.Strings(keys) sortedArray := make([]any, len(unsortedMap)) // L149: map read, unlocked for i, mapKey := range keys { sortedArray[i] = unsortedMap[mapKey] // L151: map read, unlocked } return sortedArray } ``` `SetInMap` writes into that same map while holding the write lock. A mutex protects a map only when both sides hold it during the access, so `GetSortedMapValues` running concurrently with `SetInMap` is an unsynchronized read against a write. The Go runtime treats that as fatal and aborts the process; it is not a race a program can be built to tolerate. Every other method on this type reads or writes `c.values` under the lock. This one is the outlier: it takes the lock, then does its actual work after releasing it. This is reachable from ordinary templates. `hugo.Store`, `site.Store`, `PAGE.Store` and `SHORTCODE.Store` all return `*hstore.Scratch`, `hugo.Store` is one instance shared across the whole build, and `renderPages` in `hugolib/site_render.go` renders pages concurrently over `config.GetNumWorkerMultiplier()` workers. So a site that collects into a map with `SetInMap` from a partial called per page, and enumerates it with `GetSortedMapValues` from another template, can abort mid-build. `SetInMap` and `GetSortedMapValues` are documented together as a pair on both `hugo.Store` and `site.Store` — the two build-shared scopes — and no Store documentation page mentions concurrency at all, so nothing warns a template author away from that shape. When it does abort, the build stops with a runtime panic rather than a Hugo error, no finished site is produced, and the panic names no template. The same commit will usually build cleanly on the next run, so it reads as flaky CI rather than as a defect. The sibling `Values()` carries a comment warning that using it on a shared `Scratch` "will lead to concurrency issues". `GetSortedMapValues` carries no such warning, which is part of why it reads as the safe way to get a map back out of a store. I have not built a Hugo-site reproduction, because at the site level this is nondeterministic by nature: it needs a shared store written during concurrent page rendering and read while that is still in flight, and when it fires the panic points at no template. The Go-level reproduction below pins the same two calls deterministically. ### Reproduction This uses only the exported API of `common/hstore`; nothing touches the map directly. `go.mod`: ``` module hstorerepro go 1.26.0 require github.com/gohugoio/hugo v0.164.0 ``` Run `go mod tidy` after creating it; that adds nine indirect requirements and the `go.sum` entries. `repro_test.go`: ```go package hstorerepro import ( "sync" "testing" "github.com/gohugoio/hugo/common/hstore" ) // One goroutine enumerates the map through the store's own accessor while // another writes to it through the store's own mutator. Both use only the // exported API; neither ever touches the map directly. f

title: templates.Defer: identical block bodies in different output formats share one escaping mode, chosen non-deterministically per build
body:
### What version of Hugo are you using (`hugo version`)? 
$ hugo version
hugo v0.164.0-ce2470e7012b5ab5fc4e10ebe4027e9f8d9e00dc+extended windows/amd64 BuildDate=2026-07-06T16:39:30Z VendorInfo=gohugoio
### Does this issue reproduce with the latest release? Yes. ```text hugo v0.165.0-76a5e1880ab46688155b02e99bab9be2a6134492+extended windows/amd64 BuildDate=2026-08-12T14:26:28Z VendorInfo=gohugoio ``` Over one run of 40 consecutive builds of the unchanged reproduction site below with that binary, 28 builds published the wrong value in `public/index.html` and 12 published the wrong value in `public/index.txt`. All 40 exited 0, and none printed a warning or an error. ### Summary When two templates belonging to different output formats contain byte-identical `templates.Defer` block bodies, both blocks do execute, each with its own correct output-format context. What they share is the escaping applied inside the block, and which of the two escaping modes survives changes from build to build of an unchanged site. On every build exactly one of the two outputs is therefore wrong: either an HTML page publishes a value raw that it escapes correctly a few characters earlier outside the block, or a plain-text page receives HTML entities. ### Reproduction Three files in an empty directory. No content, no modules, no external tooling. `hugo.toml`: ```toml baseURL = 'https://example.org/' title = 'defer probe' disableKinds = ['page', 'section', 'taxonomy', 'term', 'RSS', 'sitemap', 'robotsTXT'] [outputFormats.probe] mediaType = 'text/plain' baseName = 'index' isPlainText = true [outputs] home = ['html', 'probe'] ``` `layouts/home.html`: ```go-html-template {{ $v := "&" }}OUT[{{ $v }}]{{ with (templates.Defer (dict "key" "K" "data" (dict "v" $v))) }}IN[{{ .v }}]{{ end }} ``` `layouts/home.probe.txt`, byte-identical to `layouts/home.html` (both md5 `c921197a9c8637852e38d94a0352359d`): ```go-html-template {{ $v := "&" }}OUT[{{ $v }}]{{ with (templates.Defer (dict "key" "K" "data" (dict "v" $v))) }}IN[{{ .v }}]{{ end }} ``` `OUT[...]` interpolates the value outside the deferred block, `IN[...]` interpolates the same value inside it. Then run `hugo` several times without changing anything, and look at `public/index.html` and `public/index.txt` after each run. ### What happens Two consecutive runs of the same command on the unchanged site, pasted verbatim: ```text $ hugo --logLevel info Start building sites … hugo v0.164.0-ce2470e7012b5ab5fc4e10ebe4027e9f8d9e00dc+extended windows/amd64 BuildDate=2026-07-06T16:39:30Z VendorInfo=gohugoio INFO build: step process substep collect files 0 files_total 0 pagesources_total 0 resourcesources_total 0 duration 0s INFO build: step process duration 0s INFO build: step assemble duration 0s INFO build: step render substep pages site en outputFormat html duration 1.3703ms INFO build: step render substep pages site en outputFormat probe duration 509.5µs INFO build: step render pages 2 content 0 duration 1.8798ms INFO build: step render deferred count 2 duration 1.7766ms INFO build: step postProcess duration 0s INFO build: duration 4.171ms │ EN ──────────────────┼──── Pages │ 2 Paginator pages │ 0 Non-page files │ 0 Static files │ 0 Processed images │ 0 Aliases │ 0 Cleaned │ 0 Total in 12 ms --- public/index.html --- OUT[<b>&]IN[&] --- public/index.txt --- OUT[&]IN[&] ``` ```text $ hugo --logLevel info Start building sites … hugo v0.164.0-ce2470e7012b5ab5fc4e10ebe4027e9f8d9e00dc+extended windows/amd64 BuildDate=2026-07-06T16:39:30Z VendorInfo=gohugoio INFO build: step process substep collect files 0 files_total 0 pagesources_total 0 resourcesources_total 0 duration 513.8µs INFO build: step process duration 513.8µs INFO build: step assemble duration 0s INFO build: step render substep pages site en outputFormat html duration 517.9µs INFO build: step render subst

title: panic: slice bounds out of range in contentNodeShifter.Delete when removing draft pages from a multilingual taxonomy
body:
### What version of Hugo are you using?

Reproduced on both:

```
hugo v0.159.1-86c7d3afacab79dc53325602d77ef884b7570268+extended darwin/arm64
hugo v0.164.0+extended+withdeploy darwin/arm64
```

### Does this issue reproduce with the latest release?

Yes (0.164.0).

### What did you expect to see?

A production build (no `-D`) of a multilingual site containing draft pages completes.

### What did you see instead?

```
panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [5:4]

goroutine 37 [running]:
github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib.(*contentNodeShifter).Delete(0x..., {0x..., 0x...}, {0x2, 0x0, 0x0})
	github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib/content_map_page_contentnodeshifter.go:48 +0x5f4
github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib/doctree.(*NodeShiftTree[...]).delete(0x..., {0x..., 0x35})
	github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib/doctree/nodeshifttree.go:165 +0x84
github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib/doctree.(*NodeShiftTree[...]).Delete(...)
	github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib/doctree/nodeshifttree.go:107
github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib.(*allPagesAssembler).createAllPages.func1-range1(...)
	github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib/content_map_page_assembler.go:106 +0xa4
github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib.(*allPagesAssembler).createAllPages(...)
	github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib/content_map_page_assembler.go:138 +0x168
github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib.(*HugoSites).assemble(...)
	github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib/hugo_sites_build.go:345 +0x41c
```

The `0x35` in `delete(..., {…, 0x35})` is 53, exactly the byte length of the key being removed (`/blog/` plus a 47-character slug).

### Only on the page-removal path

`hugo -D` (drafts included) builds fine. The panic appears only when a page is *removed* from the tree, which makes it invisible in local preview and fatal only in production.

A **future `publishDate`** panics identically. Setting `[_build] render = "never"` / `list = "never"` on the same pages avoids it entirely — consistent with those pages never being added to the tree, so nothing is deleted.

### What I ruled out

Site: 8 languages, ~1,490 pages per language, ~11,455 content files, `categories` taxonomy.

- **Not a regression.** 0.159.1 and 0.164.0 behave identically.
- **Not the number of drafts.** 96 draft pages build fine; 16 panic.
- **Not slug length.** The panicking key was 47 chars, but renaming an unrelated post to exactly 47 chars builds fine.
- **Not the slug.** Renaming the offending page does not help.
- **Not byte layout.** Deleting a front-matter line, or adding a blank one, still panics.

Swapping page *content* at a fixed path isolates it to **front matter**. Changing `categories = ["Airport Operations"]` on the offending page to any other value clears the panic — and so does moving a *different* page out of that same category while leaving the offending one alone. So the trigger is combinatorial: some particular set of pages being deleted from one taxonomy term corrupts the shifter, rather than any single page being malformed.

### Reproducer

I have not managed to minimise it, and I want to be upfront about that. Synthetic multilingual sites (8 languages, 12 blog + 200 glossary pages sharing one taxonomy term, varying draft counts) do **not** reproduce, so something else in the real tree is required. The affected repository is private.

I am happy to run patches or instrumented builds against the real site and report back, which may be faster than guessing at a minimal case.

title: ReadingTime and FuzzyWordCount have off-by-one errors in their ceiling calculations
body:
## Summary

Two related integer-arithmetic bugs in `hugolib/page__content.go` (in the plain-content calculation), causing behavior that deviates from documented intent at boundary values.

## 1. `ReadingTime` divides by 213/501 instead of 212/500

```go
if isCJKLanguage {
    result.readingTime = (result.wordCount + 500) / 501
} else {
    result.readingTime = (result.wordCount + 212) / 213
}
```

The intent is a reading speed of 212 words per minute (500 for CJK), rounded up. But the correct ceiling-division idiom is `(n + d - 1) / d`. As written, the expression computes `ceil(wordCount / 213)` and `ceil(wordCount / 501)`, so the effective reading speeds are 213 and 501 wpm.

| wordCount | current: `(wc+212)/213` | expected at 212 wpm: `ceil(wc/212)` |
|---|---|---|
| 212 | 1 | 1 |
| 213 | **1** | **2** |
| 424 | 2 | 2 |
| 425 | **2** | **3** |

Proposed fix:

```go
result.readingTime = (result.wordCount + 211) / 212   // non-CJK
result.readingTime = (result.wordCount + 499) / 500   // CJK
```

## 2. `FuzzyWordCount` overshoots on exact multiples of 100

```go
result.fuzzyWordCount = (result.wordCount + 100) / 100 * 100
```

Documented as the word count "rounded up to the nearest multiple of 100", but adding 100 unconditionally bumps exact multiples to the *next* multiple:

| wordCount | current | expected |
|---|---|---|
| 99 | 100 | 100 |
| 100 | **200** | **100** |
| 101 | 200 | 200 |
| 0 | **100** | **0** |

Proposed fix:

```go
result.fuzzyWordCount = (result.wordCount + 99) / 100 * 100
```

Both changes only affect output at exact boundary values, but they do change rendered output for existing sites (e.g., a 100-word page's `FuzzyWordCount` drops from 200 to 100), so this may warrant a changelog note.

## Integration Test

<details>
<summary>hugolib/page_test.go</summary>

```go
// See issue 15206.
func TestReadingTimeAndFuzzyWordCountBoundaries(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()

	files := `
-- hugo.toml --
disableKinds = ["home", "section", "taxonomy", "term", "rss", "sitemap"]
-- content/p99.md --
---
title: p99
---
` + strings.Repeat("word ", 99) + `
-- content/p100.md --
---
title: p100
---
` + strings.Repeat("word ", 100) + `
-- content/p101.md --
---
title: p101
---
` + strings.Repeat("word ", 101) + `
-- content/p211.md --
---
title: p211
---
` + strings.Repeat("word ", 211) + `
-- content/p212.md --
---
title: p212
---
` + strings.Repeat("word ", 212) + `
-- content/p213.md --
---
title: p213
---
` + strings.Repeat("word ", 213) + `
-- content/p499.md --
---
title: p499
isCJKLanguage: true
---
` + strings.Repeat("你", 499) + `
-- content/p500.md --
---
title: p500
isCJKLanguage: true
---
` + strings.Repeat("你", 500) + `
-- content/p501.md --
---
title: p501
isCJKLanguage: true
---
` + strings.Repeat("你", 501) + `
-- layouts/page.html --
{{ .WordCount }}|{{ .FuzzyWordCount }}|{{ .ReadingTime }}
`

	b := Test(t, files)

	b.AssertFileContent("public/p99/index.html", "99|100|1")
	b.AssertFileContent("public/p100/index.html", "100|100|1") // fails
	b.AssertFileContent("public/p101/index.html", "101|200|1")

	b.AssertFileContent("public/p211/index.html", "211|300|1")
	b.AssertFileContent("public/p212/index.html", "212|300|1")
	b.AssertFileContent("public/p213/index.html", "213|300|2") // fails

	b.AssertFileContent("public/p499/index.html", "499|500|1")
	b.AssertFileContent("public/p500/index.html", "500|500|1") // fails
	b.AssertFileContent("public/p501/index.html", "501|600|2") // fails
}
```
</details>

title: hugo --gc deletes in-use image cache files when on-disk path case differs from the cache key (case-insensitive filesystems)
body: ### What happens On a case-insensitive filesystem (macOS APFS, Windows), `hugo --gc` deletes image cache files under `resources/_gen` that the build **actively uses**, if the on-disk path case differs from the cache key. The build itself works fine (the case-insensitive filesystem resolves the read), but the pruner's usage check is a case-sensitive string comparison, so the just-used file is considered unused and removed. The relevant code is in `cache/filecache/filecache_pruner.go` (unchanged on master): ```go if !shouldRemove && c.entryLocker.seen.Len() > 0 { // Remove it if it's not been touched/used in the last build. shouldRemove = !c.entryLocker.seen.Has(name) } ``` `seen` contains the cache key (for images: the lowercased target path, via `ImageCache.getOrCreate` → `c.fcache.ReadOrCreate(relTargetPath, …)`), while `name` is the real on-disk name from the filesystem walk. If they differ only in case, `seen.Has(name)` is false and the file is deleted. ### Why the case can differ in practice Page paths have been lowercased since the v0.123 page-system rewrite, so cache keys for page-bundle images are lowercase. Caches created by older Hugo versions preserve the source directory case (e.g. `resources/_gen/images/collections/PastFuture/…`). Such caches are common in the wild: committed to git for CI cold-start speed, restored by CI cache plugins, or simply carried forward on a developer machine across Hugo upgrades. The result is a permanent rebuild/evict cycle: `--gc` deletes the in-use entries → the next build silently re-processes all of them → the new files land inside the surviving mixed-case directory (the prune walk visits directories before deleting their files, so the directory is never seen empty and survives; on a case-insensitive filesystem the re-created file then lands in it) → the next `--gc` deletes them again. On the real site where we found this, every build re-scaled 267 images (~35 s per build, forever). ### Minimal reproduction (macOS) ```sh hugo new site repro && cd repro mkdir -p content/MyBundle layouts/_default printf 'baseURL = "https://example.org/"\ndisableKinds = ["taxonomy", "term", "rss", "sitemap"]\n' > hugo.toml printf -- '---\ntitle: My Bundle\n---\n' > content/MyBundle/index.md cp /path/to/any.jpeg content/MyBundle/cover.jpeg printf '{{ with .Resources.GetMatch "cover.jpeg" }}{{ with .Resize "100x" }}{{ end }}{{ end }}' > layouts/_default/single.html printf 'home' > layouts/_default/home.html hugo # creates resources/_gen/images/mybundle/cover_hu_.jpeg # simulate a cache written by an older Hugo (or copied from elsewhere): mv resources/_gen/images/mybundle resources/_gen/images/tmp mv resources/_gen/images/tmp resources/_gen/images/MyBundle hugo --gc # build succeeds (16 ms, cache hit), but reports "Cleaned 1" find resources -type f # -> empty: the file the build just used is gone hugo # re-processes the image (474 ms) — and writes it back # into the surviving MyBundle/ dir, so the cycle repeats ``` Observed output of the `--gc` build: ``` Processed images │ 1 Cleaned │ 1 Total in 16 ms ``` A cache file that was read 16 ms earlier is deleted as "not been touched/used in the last build". ### What I expected `--gc` should never delete a cache entry that the same build read. On case-insensitive filesystems the usage check should match the way the filesystem resolved the read — e.g. compare case-insensitively (or normalize walk names against the `seen` set) when the cache filesystem is case-insensitive. Renaming the on-disk entry to the key's case would even self-heal old caches. ### Version ``` hugo v0.164.0+extended+withdeploy darwin/arm64 BuildDate=2026-07-06T16:39:30Z VendorInfo=Homebrew ``` The pruner code is identical on current master.

title: Make template name lookup case-insensitive for layout front matter and .Render
body:
When looking up a template, the name supplied via the `layout` front matter parameter or as an argument to the `Page.Render` method is matched against file names using a case-sensitive comparison. Shortcode and partial template lookups are already case-insensitive. These should behave the same way.

Ref. @jmooring 's post here: https://discourse.gohugo.io/t/security-error-with-the-new-0-161-0-security-for-postcss/57186/16

This issue triggered in this case because of how Netlify stores its `node_modules` cache in the same tree as the Hugo file cache. This is a hard-to-debug issue for the end user and I think we need to fix this. As I understand it, I think this is only a problem with Node's CJS resolver.

E.g. when using CJS style `require` in `postcss.config.js`

```
const autoprefixer = require('autoprefixer');
module.exports = {
  plugins: [
    autoprefixer
  ]
}
```

And having a "pseudo" (very simplified) Hugo project stetup like this:

```

cache/hugo_cache/mymodule
hugo_project/node_modules/postcss

title: Multiple values in --renderSegments behaves surprisingly
body:
See https://discourse.gohugo.io/t/segmentation-question/57258

When I implemented the `--renderSegments` flag I:

* Mostly had the single segment definition in mind, e.g. `weekly`, `daily`.
* Tried to get everything into one site/page loop for performance reasons.

So currently when you say `--renderSegments blog,news`, we combine the filters of `blog` and `news` into one. This means that if you say

* blog: include `/blog/**`, exclude JSON output.
* news: include `/news/**`.

The JSON output is never rendered for any of the segments, which people find surprising.

You can currently work around this by

```
hugo --renderSegments blog
hugo --renderSegments new
```

Gziper leaks a pgzip writer goroutine and its buffers on every gzip-accepting HEAD request
body:
### Summary

On a HEAD request whose `Accept-Encoding` includes `gzip`, Grafana's `Gziper` middleware wraps the response in a `klauspost/pgzip` writer and sets `Content-Encoding: gzip`. Go's `net/http` discards the body of a HEAD response, so the writer is never closed. Its compression goroutine parks on a channel for the life of the process and keeps its block buffers reachable, so the GC cannot reclaim them.

The result is unbounded heap growth proportional to the rate of gzip-accepting HEAD requests, ending in OOM. Health checks are the common source: they are usually HEAD, usually frequent, and most HTTP clients send `Accept-Encoding: gzip` by default.

**Affected:** Grafana 13.1.4 (`github.com/klauspost/pgzip` v1.2.6). We have not tested other versions.

### Confirming it on any running instance, with no tooling attached

This needs only the metrics endpoint — no pprof, no profiling build, no restart:

```
go_goroutines
grafana_http_request_duration_seconds_count{handler="/api/health",method="HEAD"}
```

Sample both on **one pid** and compare the deltas over the same window. Do not subtract a baseline taken from a different process — goroutine counts at startup vary, and a remembered baseline will give you a ratio that is wrong in either direction. On unmodified production instances we measure **≈ 1.0 leaked goroutine per gzip-accepting HEAD request served**:

| window | pid age at start | traffic | Δ HEAD /api/health | Δ go_goroutines | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 min | 1 min | ambient only | 20 | 20 | **1.00** |
| 4 min | 5 min | ambient + a 30-request burst we issued | 59 | 59 | **1.00** |
| 2 min | 6h25m | ambient only | 41 | 31 | 0.76 |

The middle window is the controlled one: 30 of those requests were ours, issued as HEAD with `Accept-Encoding: gzip`, and the total still comes out 1:1. The other two are pure observation of an existing health-check client.

We have **not** isolated why the third window reads below 1.0. Two candidates we did not separate: its HEAD count may include probes from clients whose `Accept-Encoding` we did not control, and on a process that has been up for hours `go_goroutines` also moves with unrelated request churn. Treat a sub-1.0 ambient ratio as a lower bound rather than a measurement, and use the burst reproducer below if you want a clean number.

The growth is monotonic and never recovers.

### Minimal reproducer

Against a running Grafana, on one pid, 10s sampling of `go_goroutines`:

```bash
for i in $(seq 1 30); do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -X HEAD -H 'Accept-Encoding: gzip' http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/health
done
```

**30 requests → 30 leaked goroutines, 1:1.** Controls, same instance, same method of measurement:

| request | count | leaked goroutines |
|---|---|---|
| `HEAD /api/health` with `Accept-Encoding: gzip` | 30 | **30** |
| `HEAD /api/health` with `Accept-Encoding: identity` | 30 | 0 |
| `GET /api/health` with `Accept-Encoding: gzip` | 30 | 0 |
| `GET /api/ds/query` (202 KB response) with gzip | 5 | 0 |
| large static asset (`/public/build/*.js`) with gzip | 10 | 0 |

Only HEAD + gzip leaks, and it leaks on every request. The endpoint is incidental — any handler behind `Gziper` reproduces it.

### The response that causes it

```
$ curl -s -D - -o /dev/null -X HEAD -H 'Accept-Encoding: gzip' http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/health
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Encoding: gzip
Vary: Accept-Encoding
Content-Type: application/json; charset=UTF-8
```

`Content-Encoding: gzip` on a HEAD response, with no body to decode. Correspondingly `grafana_http_response_size_bytes_sum` for that handler is `0` — the body is discarded while the compressor is still wrapped around it.

### Retention path

Goroutine profile — 183 goroutines parked on the same frame, growing linearly:

```
183 @ 0x491eee 0x41eeae 0x41e9f2 0x67a1974 0x49a741
#	github.com/klauspost/pgzip.(*Writer).Write.func1+0x53   pgzip@v1.2.6/gzip.go:364
```

title: fix(dashboards): support long v2 metadata names in git-sync
body:
Fixes #132220.

Grafana v2 dashboard metadata.name follows Kubernetes naming rules and can be longer than the legacy dashboard UID limit. During conversion to the legacy v1 dashboard representation, that name was copied directly into the legacy UID and git-sync failed with `uid too long, max 40 characters`.

This change keeps the v2 metadata.name unchanged and, only when converting a v2 dashboard to the legacy v1 representation, derives a deterministic 40-character SHA-256-based UID when the name is not a valid legacy UID. Short valid names are preserved unchanged.

Added regression coverage for long names and Kubernetes-style names containing dots.

Implementation and tests are already present in `devanshpandey-08/grafana` on branch `fix/132220-gitsync-long-dashboard-name`.

title: Analyzer suggest incorrect UpperCamelCase for structs with keyword name
body:
While looking at rust documentation, I discovered that you could name things after keywords by adding `r#` as prefix, ex: `let r#pub: i32 = 5;`. Very suprised, I tried to do it (and of course it worked), but when trying it with a struct name, like this:
```rust
struct r#pub;
```
It didn't throw any errors, but rust-analyzer complained saying that I should use UpperCamelCase:
```
Structure `r#pub` should have UpperCamelCase name, e.g. `R#pub`
```
But that's incorrect, it should suggest either `Pub` or `r#Pub`, but not `R#pub`. And when trying to compile, the compiler gives a correct warning of:
```
struct r#pub;
       ^^^^^ help: convert the identifier to upper camel case: `Pub`
```


Also, I'm sorry but I'm using rust-analyzer on nvf (neovim configured with nix), and I don't know how to check its version. But I did try to check if there were any similar issues and didn't see any, closed or otherwise.

If this is not reproducible, I will try to dig around to find the versions of all the things I used.

title: False E0608 when indexing an array in a let initializer
body:
## Description

rust-analyzer incorrectly reports E0608 for valid array indexing expressions used as `let` initializers.

The same indexing expression does not produce an error when used inside `println!`.

`cargo check` succeeds without any errors.

## Reproduction

```rust
fn main() {
    let a = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];

    let first = a[0];
    let second = a[1];

    println!("{}", a[1]);
}
````

rust-analyzer reports:

```text
error[E0608]: cannot index into a value of type `[i32; 5]`
```

on both:

```rust
let first = a[0];
let second = a[1];
```

However, this does not produce an E0608 diagnostic:

```rust
println!("{}", a[1]);
```

The type of `a` is correctly shown as `[i32; 5]` when hovering over it in VS Code.

`cargo check` succeeds:

```text
warning: unused variable: `first`
warning: unused variable: `second`
Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.01s
```

The warnings are only because the two variables are unused.

## Environment

* OS: Arch Linux
* rustc: `rustc 1.98.0 (88d9e12ae 2026-08-18) (Arch Linux rust 1:1.98.0-1)`
* cargo: `cargo 1.98.0 (797e8a9bc 2026-08-05) (Arch Linux rust 1:1.98.0-1)`
* rust-analyzer: `rust-analyzer 0.4.3023-standalone`
* VS Code extension: `rust-lang.rust-analyzer@0.4.3023`
* Editor: VS Code

No custom rust-analyzer configuration is required to reproduce the issue.

## Expected behavior

All array indexing expressions should be accepted without an E0608 diagnostic.

## Actual behavior

`a[0]` and `a[1]` produce a false E0608 diagnostic when used as `let` initializers, while the same `a[1]` expression inside `println!` does not.

`cargo check` accepts all of them.

This appears to be related to rust-analyzer issue #22628, although this reproduction does not use `no_std`, a custom target, or `Vec`.

title: --lockfile-path is passed to pre-release toolchains in the 1.95 / 1.97 bands
body:
**editor or extension**: VSCode, `rust-lang.rust-analyzer` extension `0.3.3016`
 
**relevant settings**:
 
```jsonc
{
  "rust-analyzer.server.extraEnv": { "RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN": "esp" },
  "rust-analyzer.cargo.extraEnv":  { "RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN": "esp" },
  "rust-analyzer.cargo.target": "xtensa-esp32-none-elf",
  "rust-analyzer.cargo.allTargets": false,
  "rust-analyzer.check.allTargets": false
}
```
 
`CARGO`, `CARGO_HOME` and `RUSTUP_HOME` are unset. The `esp` toolchain is the Xtensa fork
installed by [espup](https://github.com/esp-rs/espup); it is selected here via a
`rust-toolchain.toml` containing `channel = "esp"`, and the `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN` settings above
are redundant with that.
 
**repository link (if public, optional)**: n/a — reproduces on any Cargo project, see below
 
**code snippet to reproduce**:
 
```rust
// No particular code is needed — this is a project-loading failure, not an analysis one.
// Any Cargo project will do, as long as the active toolchain reports a *pre-release*
// version in the 1.95 band, e.g.:
//
//   $ cargo --version
//   cargo 1.95.0-nightly (f2d3ce0bd 2026-03-21)
//
// A plain `rustup toolchain install nightly` from the 1.95 cycle reproduces it;
// so does espup's `esp` channel, which is what I hit it on.
fn main() {}
```
 
---
 
## Summary
 
`make_lockfile_copy` selects the lockfile-redirection mechanism by comparing the parsed
toolchain version against thresholds declared with `pre: semver::Prerelease::EMPTY`. Semver
orders a pre-release *below* its release, so a toolchain whose version equals a threshold but
carries a pre-release tag falls into the band **below** it.
 
On cargo `1.95.0-nightly` this selects `LockfileUsage::WithFlag`, so rust-analyzer passes
`--lockfile-path` — the flag cargo 1.95 replaced with `CARGO_RESOLVER_LOCKFILE_PATH`.
 
## Impact
 
`cargo metadata` fails and rust-analyzer falls back to `--no-deps`. This is logged only at
`WARN`, and the server otherwise starts and reports a healthy workspace — but both the
workspace metadata fetch *and* `Sysroot::load_workspace` fail, so **no dependency crates and
no sysroot crates are indexed**. Every path in the project resolves to nothing, including
`core`. It presents as a broken project rather than a degraded fetch, which makes it hard to
attribute to this cause.
 
## Reproduction
 
```console
$ cargo --version
cargo 1.95.0-nightly (f2d3ce0bd 2026-03-21) (1.95.0.0)
 
$ cargo metadata --format-version 1 --lockfile-path /tmp/ra-test.lock
error: unexpected argument '--lockfile-path' found
 
  tip: a similar argument exists: '--locked'
 
Usage: cargo metadata --format-version <VERSION> --filter-platform <TRIPLE> --locked
```
 
Server log — repeats for the workspace and again for the sysroot on every load:
 
```
WARN `cargo metadata` failed and returning succeeded result with `--no-deps`
  error=`cargo metadata` exited with an error: error: unexpected argument '--lockfile-path' found
  ...
   2: <project_model::cargo_workspace::FetchMetadata>::exec
   3: std::sys::backtrace::__rust_begin_short_backtrace::<...load_cargo...>
 
WARN `cargo metadata` failed and returning succeeded result with `--no-deps`
  ...
   2: <project_model::cargo_workspace::FetchMetadata>::exec
   3: <project_model::sysroot::Sysroot>::load_workspace
```
 
## Cause
 
`crates/project-model/src/toolchain_info/version.rs` parses the version, keeping the
pre-release tag:
 
```rust
let version =
    out.strip_prefix(prefix).and_then(|it| Version::parse(it.split_whitespace().next()?).ok());
```
 
`cargo 1.95.0-nightly (f2d3ce0bd 2026-03-21) (1.95.0.0)` → `Version { major: 1, minor: 95,
patch: 0, pre: "nightly" }`.
 
`crates/project-model/src/cargo_config_file.rs` then compares it against three thresholds, all
of which use `Prerelease::EMPTY`:
 
```rust
const MINIMUM_TOOLCHAIN_VERSION_SUPPORTING_LOCKFILE_PATH_FLAG: semver::Version =
    semver::Version { major: 1, minor: 82, patch: 0, pre: semver::Prerelease::EMPTY, .. };
 
const MINIMUM_TOOLCHAIN_VERSION_SUPPORTING_LOCKF

Troubleshooting guide: https://rust-analyzer.github.io/book/troubleshooting.html

Before submitting, please make sure that you're not running into one of these known issues:

Otherwise please try to provide information which will help us to fix the issue faster. Minimal reproducible examples with few dependencies are especially lovely <3.
-->

`format!()` in an async block is non-send. It compiles successfully, but RA raise an error.

**rust-analyzer version**: rust-analyzer 1.99.0-nightly (87e5904 2026-07-20) .. rustc 1.100.0-nightly (67854e511 2026-08-15)

**rustc version**: rustc 1.99.0-nightly (ba28ff76f 2026-08-13) .. rust-analyzer 1.100.0-nightly (67854e5 2026-08-15)

**editor or extension**: neovim 0.12.2 / Linux NixOS

**code snippet to reproduce**:
```rust
#[allow(unused)]
fn fun() {
    async fn inner() {
        let foo = String::from("foo");

        let bar = format!("bar{foo}");
    }

    let future = inner();

    fn check<T: Future + Send>(value: T) {}

    check(future);
    //^^^
    // Diagnostics:
    // 1. the trait bound `NonNull<()>: Send` is not satisfied
    //    required by the bound `ArgumentType<'<erased>>: Send`
    //    required by the bound `Argument<'<erased>>: Send`
    //    required by the bound `[Argument<'<erased>>; 1]: Send`
    //    required by the bound `&mut [Argument<'<erased>>; 1]: Send`
    //    required by the bound `(&mut String, &mut (&String,), &mut [Argument<'<erased>>; 1]): Send`
    //    required by the bound `impl Future<Output = ()>: Send`
    //    required by the bound `impl Future<Output = ()>: Send`
    //     [E0277]

}
```

---

Update: After a quick check found out that the error starts appearing at `rust-analyzer 1.99.0-nightly (87e5904 2026-07-20)`, before that version (`<= rust-analyzer 1.99.0-nightly (9f36de7 2026-07-19)`) it's working fine

ci: io_uring latest-kernel leg reports "all tests passed" after `fs_uring` is OOM-killed inside QEMU; the remaining test binaries never run, and `fs_uring_statx::stat_permission_denied` fails once they do
body:
The `Test io_uring on Linux <latest-stable>` job ([`uring-kernel-version-test.yml`](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/blob/d6bf379eba23fbe2dc334b2da4e3d28ee65e5ffd/.github/workflows/uring-kernel-version-test.yml), called from `ci.yml` on every push and PR) is green on every retained master run, but inside the guest `fs_uring` is OOM-killed during `open_many_files`, init dies with it, and the 10 binaries that sort after it (the other `fs_uring_*` suites, `fs_write`, and the `tokio` lib test binary) never execute. The step still prints `all tests passed` because a SIGKILLed binary never writes the `test result: FAILED` line the step greps for, and QEMU exits 0 after the resulting kernel panic under `panic=1 -no-reboot`. Giving the guest enough memory shows what the green was hiding: `fs_uring_statx::stat_permission_denied` fails on 7.2.4, because the guest runs the tests as root and a `0o244` directory does not stop root. The job exists to "run fs tests on the latest linux kernel, ensuring tokio's io_uring apis don't break on the latest kernel" (#7486).

**Reproduction**, from the latest master run [34219362392](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/actions/runs/34219362392) (d6bf379e):

```
gh run view 34219362392 -R tokio-rs/tokio --job 102039005349 --log \
  | grep -E 'running [0-9]+ tests?|Out of memory|Attempted to kill init|all tests passed'
```

On the 7.2.4 job ([102039005349](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/actions/runs/34219362392/job/102039005349)) this prints 15 `running N tests` lines, then:

```
test open_many_files ... [   72.915500] tokio-rt-worker invoked oom-killer: ...
[   72.927912] Out of memory: Killed process 175 (fs_uring-da0323) total-vm:285332kB, anon-rss:205708kB, file-rss:31116kB, ...
[   72.970629] Kernel panic - not syncing: Attempted to kill init! exitcode=0x00008900
all tests passed
```

The 4.19.325 control job in the same run ([102039005534](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/actions/runs/34219362392/job/102039005534)) prints 25 `running N tests` lines, including `running 200 tests` for the lib binary, before `Attempted to kill init! exitcode=0x00000000` and `all tests passed`.

**Mechanism.** init runs `for f in /bin/tests/*; do RUST_BACKTRACE=1 "$f" ; done` under `set -e` ([L74–L83](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/blob/d6bf379eba23fbe2dc334b2da4e3d28ee65e5ffd/.github/workflows/uring-kernel-version-test.yml#L74-L83)). `fs_uring` sorts first among the io_uring binaries (`-` before `_`), and `open_many_files` (512 files, 10 000 spawned opens, [`fs_uring.rs#L88-L98`](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/blob/d6bf379eba23fbe2dc334b2da4e3d28ee65e5ffd/tokio/tests/fs_uring.rs#L88-L98)) reaches 200–340 MB anon RSS in a `-m 1024` guest where ~746 MiB is already unevictable, because the initramfs holds the unstripped musl debug binaries (cpio archive 1 528 706 blocks, ≈783 MB). The kernel kills the test, init exits 137, the kernel panics (`exitcode=0x00008900`), and with `panic=1` + `-no-reboot` QEMU shuts down with status 0, so the `qemu_status` check from #8271 passes (`-action panic=exit-failure` changes nothing: the 4.19 leg also ends in `Attempted to kill init` and QEMU exits 0 there too). The last gate, `grep -q "test result: FAILED"` ([L115](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/blob/d6bf379eba23fbe2dc334b2da4e3d28ee65e5ffd/.github/workflows/uring-kernel-version-test.yml#L115)), cannot see a binary killed before it printed a summary. #8271's description names exactly this gap: "The log check only recognizes Rust's `test result: FAILED` text, so it is not a substitute for QEMU's exit status" — and #8271's own merge run has the same OOM kill under a green step.

The pattern is identical in the oldest retained latest-kernel log and at a midpoint, so it is at least 77 days old; the onset is beyond log retention:

- 2026-06-23, kernel 7.1.1, job [82908203355](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/actions/runs/28010858949/job/82908203355): `Killed process 172 (fs_uring-dface4) ... anon-rss:337824kB`, `exitcode=0x00

title: Tests in tokio/tests/tracing_task.rs are flaky on master (~10% of runs)
body:
Three of the six tests in `tokio/tests/tracing_task.rs` fail intermittently on a clean master, with no changes applied. It has been showing up as red CI on pull requests that touch nothing related.

Measured on `ea91b33c`, macOS arm64, 105 consecutive runs of the whole test binary: 10 failures, about 9.5%.

`task_big_spawn_sizes_recorded` accounted for 7 of them, `task_spawn_sizes_recorded` for 2, and `task_builder_loc_file_recorded` for 1.

Reproduction:

```sh
git worktree add /tmp/wt master && cd /tmp/wt
for i in $(seq 1 60); do
  RUSTFLAGS="--cfg tokio_unstable" cargo test -q -p tokio \
    --features full,tracing --test tracing_task 2>&1 \
    | grep -q "test result: ok" || echo "run $i FAILED"
done
```

Running a single test on its own passes consistently; the failures only appear when the whole binary runs, which is when the six tests execute in parallel.

The failure for `task_big_spawn_sizes_recorded` is always the same shape. Its mock subscriber receives a `runtime.resource` span while it is still expecting `runtime.spawn`:

```
[task_big_spawn_sizes_recorded] expected a new span named `runtime.spawn`,
[task_big_spawn_sizes_recorded] but got one named `runtime.resource` instead.
thread 'task_big_spawn_sizes_recorded' panicked at tokio/tests/tracing_task.rs:169:14:
failed to await join handle: JoinError::Panic(Id(4), ...)
```

I have not captured the message for the other two tests, so I cannot say yet whether they fail the same way.

What makes this look like cross-test interference rather than a single bad test: `task_spawn_sizes_recorded` spawns `futures::future::ready(())` and never touches a timer, so it has no `runtime.resource` span of its own to receive. `task_big_spawn_sizes_recorded` is the only test in the file that awaits `tokio::time::sleep`, and `Sleep` is instrumented with a `runtime.resource` span at `tokio/src/time/sleep.rs:262`.

Running the same binary with `--test-threads=1` passed 60 out of 60. So this is interference between the tests, not a bad test.

I tried to narrow it further and ruled out four things, all measured rather than reasoned:

- **Cross-thread subscriber installation.** Each test uses `tracing::subscriber::set_default`, which is thread-local, and `#[tokio::test]` defaults to a current-thread runtime. Tokio does not propagate a `Dispatch` into spawned tasks.
- **The `runtime.resource` span from `Sleep`.** Replacing the `tokio::time::sleep` in `task_big_spawn_sizes_recorded` with `yield_now` did not help: 7 failures in 120 runs. It only changed the symptom, from receiving the wrong span to `more notifications expected`, i.e. the `runtime.spawn` span never arriving at all. Both symptoms are the same underlying miss.
- **Callsite interest caching via `Interest::never()`.** `tracing-mock`'s `register_callsite` returns `always()`/`never()` and never `sometimes()`, so this looked promising, but `subscriber::mock()`'s default filter is `|_| true` and its `max_level` is `None`, so nothing takes the `never()` branch.
- **Concurrency itself.** Serialising the six tests behind a `Mutex`, so they never overlap, still failed 9 times in 150 runs.

That last one is the interesting one. `--test-threads=1` fixes it and a mutex does not, and the difference between them is not whether the tests overlap but *which thread they run on*: one shared thread with a single thread-local dispatcher slot, versus six threads with six. That points at the interaction between scoped dispatchers and `tracing-core`'s global callsite state, but I could not pin it down further.

It is not specific to macOS or to arm64. The FreeBSD x86_64 job on #8388, a pull request that changes `tokio::fs` and touches nothing tracing related, failed on `task_big_spawn_sizes_recorded` with the same wrong-span message: https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/actions/runs/32831674154/job/97752105373

I could not find a fix on the tokio side that holds up under measurement, so I am reporting it rather than guessing. Happy to send a PR if you ca

title: SemaphorePermit::merge can overflow and lose permits
duplex(0) / zero-capacity in-memory pipe deadlocks on any write
body:
**Version**
tokio master (latest)

**Platform**
Any (not platform-specific)

**Description**

Creating an in-memory pipe with a buffer size of 0 — `tokio::io::duplex(0)`, `simplex(0)`, or `SimplexStream::new_unsplit(0)` — deadlocks forever on the first non-empty write. The writer waits for free buffer space, the reader waits for data, but with a 0-byte buffer neither can ever happen.

I tried this code (it hangs forever):

```rust
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let (mut a, mut b) = tokio::io::duplex(0);
    tokio::join!(
        async { a.write_all(b"x").await.unwrap(); },
        async { let mut buf = [0u8; 1]; b.read(&mut buf).await.unwrap(); },
    );
}
```

I confirmed it hangs by wrapping it in a timeout, which always elapses.

Cause: in poll_write_internal (tokio/src/io/util/mem.rs), avail = max_buf_size - buffer.len() is always 0 when max_buf_size == 0, so every write registers a waker and returns Pending with no way to make progress.

Proposed fix: reject max_buf_size == 0 with a panic at construction, matching mpsc::channel(0) which already panics with "mpsc bounded channel requires buffer > 0". Happy to send a PR.

title: multi_thread runtime deadlocks after Windows sleep/resume: all workers condvar-parked, IO/timer driver left unowned
body:
**Version**

- tokio 1.53.1 (`multi_thread`, default `#[tokio::main]`, 8 workers on 8 logical CPUs)
- mio 1.2.2
- rustc x86_64-pc-windows-msvc v1.97.0
- Windows 11 build 26200 (x64), observed on multiple machines (Dell XPS 13 9300 for the repro below)

**Platform**

Windows only as far as we can tell. Long-running network service under
continuous TCP load (transparent proxy: high accept rate, thousands of
short-lived relayed connections per hour, plus periodic timers).

A system-wide L4 proxy, built with rama#2c89a462078ba09615a204478b348ad6b80d95c1 , should that info matter.

**Description**

After the machine sleeps (modern standby, ~25 min in the repro) and
resumes, the runtime freezes completely within seconds of serving its
first post-resume work: timers stop firing, IO completions are no
longer processed, and accept loops go dead (the OS keeps completing
TCP handshakes into the listener backlog, so connects against the
service "succeed" and then hang — which is how production notices).

A minidump taken while hung shows a consistent picture:

- all 8 `tokio-rt-worker` threads are parked in
  `ntdll!ZwWaitForAlertByThreadId <= ntdll!RtlWaitOnAddress <=
  KERNELBASE!WaitOnAddress` :  for example std condvar park, **each on a
  distinct address** (per-parker, so not lock contention), with a
  **NULL timeout** (infinite wait);
- **no thread in the process is blocked in
  `NtRemoveIoCompletion(Ex)`/`GetQueuedCompletionStatusEx` on the
  runtime's IOCP** (the only IOCP waiter is winsock's internal
  `mswsock!SockAsyncThread`):  the IO/timer driver is unowned;
- the main thread is parked in `block_on` (shutdown signal wait, as
  expected), no worker thread is missing or crashed, no panic
  occurred, memory is healthy;
- among the 8 workers there are two distinct park call sites
  (6 workers share one caller chain, 2 share another), which smells
  like `Parker::park` condvar path reached from two spots in
  `multi_thread::worker`.

So the scheduler is in a state where every worker believes someone
else will wake it, and nobody holds the driver: the invariant "at
least one parked worker polls the driver (or a timeout-bounded park
exists)" is broken. The process then stays frozen indefinitely —
except that occasionally it fixes itself when an *external* thread
happens to wake a task (in our case a `DnsQueryEx` completion
callback on the OS threadpool calling `Waker::wake`, which injects
and unparks a worker). That it recovers via a remote wake suggests
lost notification / bookkeeping desync rather than corrupted state.

No `block_in_place` or nested `block_on` anywhere in the codebase;
blocking work goes through `spawn_blocking`.

My working hypothesis is that the full-process thread freeze/thaw of
suspend-resume lands in a window of the park/driver-handoff dance
(worker releasing the driver lock, peers deciding whether to take it
or condvar-park) that doesn't re-establish a driver owner on thaw.
Timing around suspend is extreme: all threads stop atomically for
minutes and resume with a burst of overdue timers + queued IOCP
completions.

**Repro**

Not minimal yet, but reliable for us: run a multi_thread runtime with
steady TCP accept/relay traffic and periodic timers, sleep the machine
(S0 modern standby) for ~15-30 min, resume, keep traffic flowing. The
hang typically forms within seconds of resume. We're working on a
minimal repro; happy to test patches or instrumented builds against
the real workload in the meantime, and can share the minidump plus
fully symbolized stacks privately.

Severity for us: high, the frozen runtime takes the host's network
down (it's a transparent proxy) until an external watchdog restarts
the process. This is something we do already but it still means affected
customers have a couple of mins of a non-functioning network

body:
### Describe the problem

As of #12821, we [error on invalid component names](https://svelte-5-preview.vercel.app/#H4sIAAAAAAAAE6tWSsvMSS1WsoquVspLzE1VslJyLChQ0lEqqSwAcYrLUnNKUoH84vzSomSQiI1zfm5Bfl5qXkm0YayCvh1QLjc_JTMtMzVFyaqkqDS1NrYWACD05ZdWAAAA). We don't have any similar validation for element names.

In Svelte 4, something like `<yes[no]>` [is a runtime error](https://svelte.dev/repl/aea07590a9ca42aabb4441106d5d4019?version=4.2.18), because you can't do this:

```js
document.createElement('yes[no]');
```

Because we use template cloning in Svelte 5, we don't hit that constraint — it just lets you create an obviously-incorrect element. We should have some validation here

### Describe the proposed solution

Either replace the 'invalid component name' error with a more generic 'invalid tag name' error, or have some way of determining whether a tag name is supposed to be a component or an element before we've been able to determine whether it's valid

title: Svelte 5: deprecate `<svelte:component>`
body:
### Describe the problem

See #12646 — we're now in a position to deprecate `<svelte:component>` if we want.

There are some places where _in theory_ it still makes sense to keep it:

```svelte
<script>
  import A from './A.svelte';
  import B from './B.svelte';

  let { condition } = $props();
</script>

<svelte:component this={condition ? A : B} />
```

```svelte
{#each things as thing}
  <svelte:component this={thing.component} />
{/each}
```

We could solve these with `$derived` or `@const` but maybe that's not as nice. The second one could be solved by treating `<thing.component>` as a component rather than as an (impossible) element, which is a change we could make separately or at the same time. (It would conflict with Svelte Native's [property elements](https://svelte-native.technology/docs#property-element), however.)

Both should be considered for 5.0

see above

title: Svelte 5: decide on behaviour of `$state.frozen`
body:
### Describe the problem

The discussion in #12413 revealed some differences of opinion around `$state.frozen`. As of that PR, it will error if passed existing reactive state, which eliminates one source of confusion. But others remain:

- in dev, the input will be frozen with `Object.freeze`, but in prod it won't (for perf reasons). As such, the name is a bit of a misnomer
- `Object.freeze` is so-called for a reason — it freezes the object passed in; it has a side-effect. `frozen` implies that it returns a frozen object, rather than freezing its argument as a side-effect. Which _isn't_ to say that `$state.freeze` would be a better name, since that implies that it freezes existing state proxies
- It's shallow — it doesn't affect state inside the object, including in classes

### Describe the proposed solution

Together, these observations suggest (to me at least) we should change the name and the behaviour. Taking a cue from [MobX](https://mobx.js.org/api.html#observableref), perhaps `$state.ref` would be a better name. `$state.raw` is another option. Doubtless there are others.

This would have similar semantics to `$state.frozen` today — in other words only reassigning (not mutating) will cause updates (or in implementation terms: it creates a source but not a proxy) — but without the dev-time `Object.freeze`.

Of course, by doing this we lose the opportunity to tell people that they're incorrectly mutating an object. If we want to keep that but _also_ have consistency between dev and prod, then the alternative is to _always_ use `Object.freeze`, perf implications be damned.

### Importance

nice to have

title: Dev-time check for `{@html ...}` mismatch
body:
### Describe the problem In a case like this... ```svelte
{browser ? 'browser' : 'server'}
``` ...Svelte will update the text node upon hydration. It does _not_ update `{@html ...}` tags however: ```svelte
{@html browser ? 'browser' : 'server'}
``` This is deliberate — these often contain large chunks of HTML rendered from a CMS or a markdown file, and as such it's very rare that there's a discrepancy between server and client. It would be expensive to either a) check that everything matches or b) remove it and reinsert it. We make a similar trade-off in the case of things like `src` attributes, since we don't want to reload iframes or kick off additional network requests. But in those cases we warn about the discrepancy at dev time. It would be nice to do the same thing for `{@html ...}` tags. ### Describe the proposed solution At dev time, hash the content and put the hash in the opening hydration boundary comment. In the browser, repeat, and check that the hashes match. ### Importance nice to have

Allow more flexible glob matchers for runic js/ts modules
body:
### Describe the problem

When you want to write runic code outside `.svelte` files you require to use the `.svelte.js` or `.svelte.ts` extension. This is fine and benefits compile times. 

The issue with this is that it can easily conflict with other libraries/frameworks that also utilize files extensions, in my case: Vitest.
Sveltekit by default through the `npm create svelte` CLI adds the following matchers:
```js
export default defineConfig({
	plugins: [sveltekit()],
	test: {
		include: ['src/**/*.{test,spec}.{js,ts}']
	}
});
```
This means when you require runic code inside test files you need to first rename your test file to `.test.svelte.ts` and then add the matcher to the vite config. Not only is this tedious but VSCode extensions like Vitest also don't understand this extra file extension which hurts the DX quite a bit for writing runic code/tests.
(Yes, you need runes inside test files because you might test a module that receives some state)

### Describe the proposed solution

The solution would be that the compiler uses a more flexible matcher for compiling js/ts files, of the top of my head I came up with: `*.svelte.*{js,ts}`.
Here are a couple of test cases that showcase the matches:
```
svelte-module.ts // ignored
module-svelte.ts // ignored
svelte.module.ts // ignored
module.svelte.ts // match
module.svelte.test.ts // match
module.test.svelte.ts // match
```
This allows for more flexible file names that don't degrade the experience with testing. I'm sure there are more frameworks/libraries that also utilize file extensions (potentially storybook) so I wouldn't say this is an edge case but a pretty common use case.

A bonus would be if when checking the Vitest option through the CLI scaffolds these matchers.

### Importance

would make my life easier

title: Rename `$derived.call` to `$derived.lazy`
body:
### Describe the problem

In #10240 we added `$derived.call(fn)` alongside `$derived(expression)`, and somehow overlooked the fact that `Function.prototype.call` is a thing.

Strictly speaking this is fine — these are runes, not functions, and we can do what the hell we want. But realistically this is going to be a source of confusion at best and annoyance at worst for many people.

### Describe the proposed solution

Programmers often talk about 'lazy evaluation', which basically means providing a function to compute some value rather than the value itself.

Even though the under-the-hood mechanism of `$derived` is that it's _always_ lazy, meaning that this...

```js
let value = $derived(expression);
```

...is syntactic sugar for this...

```js
let value = $derived.call(() => expression);
```

...I think the conceptual framing is the right one. I therefore propose `$derived.lazy`:

```js
let a = $derived(expression); // evaluated eagerly
let b = $derived.lazy(() => expression); // evaluated lazily
```

We'll also need to add an error message for anyone who is already using `$derived.call`, of course.

### Importance

would make my life easier

title: Svelte 5: Allow more flexibility for `@render` tag expressions
body:
### Describe the problem

In React, if you have a `<Button>` component, you can spread its `children` into a `<button>` and it works fine.

```jsx
function Button({ foo, ...props }) {
    return <button {...props} />;
}
```

In Svelte, we have to do this:
```svelte
<script>
    let { children } = $props();
</script>

<button>
    {#if children}
        {@render children()}
    {/if}
</button>
```
It's quite boilerplate-y.

### Describe the proposed solution

Allow passing `children` to HTML elements.
```svelte
<script>
    let { children } = $props();
</script>

<button {children} />
```

### Alternatives considered

Just keep the current syntax, which is a tad bit boilerplate-y, but not a huge deal.

### Importance

nice to have

title: Debounced Binding
body:
### Describe the problem

While creating [this example REPL](https://svelte.dev/repl/6f543749f2f24e4fb28427dec562fd8a?version=4.2.0) about how to create a timer, I came to realize that directly binding an input field to the variable that triggers the start of the timer results in an immediate start of the timer.  But what if the user is not done typing?  Then the timer continuously restarts with every keystroke.

Not only does this look "bad" in a sense, but it is a performance hit.

So what's the usual option?  To debounce the `input` event, but oh oh!  I'm not handling the input event.  I am using value binding.  I have no place to debounce.

### Describe the proposed solution

It would be ideal if Svelte could provide debouncing on binding.  Something like this:

```html
<input type="number" bind:value|debounced={variable} /> <!-- default debounce time.  400ms? -->
<input type="number" bind:value|debounced={[variable, debounceTime]} />
```

In the example, `variable` is the bound variable, while `debouncedTime` is a variable containing the number of milliseconds to debounce the binding event.

### Alternatives considered

### Drop Binding

The obvious one:  Renounce the excellent Svelte feature and instead handle the `input` event in the "classic" way.

### Bind to another Variable.

In the example REPL, the bound variable is `countFrom`.  This is passed to the Timer component, which triggers the timer.  In order to debounce this, bind the input field to a new variable, and then use reactivity (`$:`) to start the debounce.  On timeout, the variable `countFrom` would be updated.

### Importance

would make my life easier

title: Should Svelte/SvelteKit expose which versions are running?
body:
### Context

Tools like Wappalyzer use heuristics to determine which technologies are used on a given page. Some of them can be a bit brittle. For example Svelte is [detected](https://github.com/wappalyzer/wappalyzer/blob/e0c0009302ec8880aa24217dd7281898a9833b40/src/technologies/s.json#L6665) via the `svelte-` CSS scoping classname prefix...

```js
"dom": "[class*='svelte-']"
```

...which only works for apps that use Svelte's built-in CSS scoping (rather than, say, Tailwind). This mechanism is also subject to change in future, at which point the heuristic will fail.

There's also no way to know which _version_ of Svelte (or SvelteKit) is running. This information is potentially useful (hypothetical use cases: devtools, tracking the speed of adoption of new versions, reaching out to sites that are running a version with a known vulnerability) and, in fact, the [CWV tech report](https://httparchive.org/reports/cwv-tech) plans to add version information to the report in future. Currently, Svelte is systematically underrepresented in reports of technology usage, and will be excluded altogether from these more granular reports.

The question under discussion here is whether Svelte and SvelteKit should expose information about whether they're being used on a given page, and if so, whether they should expose which versions are in use.

## Security and privacy

Of course, exposing version information provides potential attackers with information about which sites to target, if a version with a known vulnerability exists. Having said that, both client-side libraries and servers have been exposing version information for many years (see e.g. a default Apache 404 page, or log `_.VERSION` on any site running Underscore), and to my knowledge this isn't a practice that's frowned upon.

If we _do_ deem granular version information to be too sensitive, then there are alternatives (which might differ between Svelte and SvelteKit — for example we could provide major/minor/patch for Svelte but only major for SvelteKit):

- expose nothing
- expose a boolean ('this site is running some version of Svelte/SvelteKit')
- expose a major version ('this site is running Svelte 4 and SvelteKit 2')
- expose major/minor
- expose major/minor/patch

Crucially, an explicit mechanism (as opposed to a heuristic based on implementation details) can have an opt-out mechanism, so exposing the boolean is arguably _more_ privacy/security conscious than the status quo (and certainly not _less_).

For this to be at all useful, it would have to be opt-out rather than opt-in.

### Implementation

For Svelte, we could add something like this to an internal module...

```js
// svelte/internal/tracking.js
(window.__svelte_versions ??= []).push(VERSION);
```

...and then import that module in every compiled component (unless the compiler were configured to opt out):

```js
import 'svelte/internal/tracking';
```

For SvelteKit, it would be natural to use the `<meta name="generator">` tag, which is used by things like Wordpress:

```html
<meta name="generator" content="SvelteKit 1.20.0">
```

### Should we do this?

The consensus among maintainers was that exposing a boolean (with an opt-out) for both Svelte and SvelteKit would make sense, since it would simply be a more reliable and privacy-forward version of existing detection mechanisms. We're undecided about whether or not we should expose version information, however.

It's important to us that decisions like these happen with the community's consent and consultation, so we'd very much welcome your thoughts on this question.

*This post has been edited, so the first couple of replies might not make much sense*

title: Duplicate `head` elements occur when html comments are stripped
body:
### Describe the bug

The [solution](https://github.com/sveltejs/svelte/pull/7745) to the duplicate content `svelte:head` element [bug](https://github.com/sveltejs/svelte/issues/6463) (and also [this one](https://github.com/sveltejs/svelte/issues/6463)) requires HTML comments to be present in order to function correctly. Many [minification tools strip HTML comments](https://github.com/sveltejs/kit/issues/7493#issuecomment-1303218382), and as does CloudFlare by default in many environments.

Duplicating the `head` element is a fairly insidious bug because it isn't immediately obvious that anything is wrong, but for our project (in SvelteKit) it decreased performance by loading analytics scripts multiple times. We also suspect that it may have broken some web indexing, but couldn't be sure.

If there is a better way to solve this than relying on comments, that would be great. I've marked the `Severity` as `annoyance`, but only because we have found a highly unsatisfactory workaround that I would rather not have in place long term.

### Reproduction

One straightforward way to reproduce this would be to use the [reproduction repo](https://github.com/thousandsofraccoons/double-meta) provided in [this issue](https://github.com/sveltejs/kit/issues/7493), which minifies the html response and strips comments: when comments are stripped, the duplicate header bug is present.

title: Feature Request: Allow nullish values to omit event handlers
body:
### Describe the problem

Most props can be excluded in this sort of fashion:
```svelte
<MyComponent
  prop={condition ? someValue : undefined}
/>
```

However, this does not work for event handlers (at least in TS setups) due to the expected TypeScript type `(e: MouseEvent) => any`.

### Describe the proposed solution

I propose setting up event handlers in such a way that they support the types `null | undefined` as well as `(e: MouseEvent) => any` and that in the case of `null | undefined`, the handler be excluded from the element/component instance.

### Alternatives considered

Currently, to work around this, I am using an "empty" function with nullish coalescing. This won't kill site performance by any means, but firing a pointless function like this is not the ideal workaround.

Here is an example of my current setup:
```svelte
<MyComponent
  prop={condition ? someValue : undefined}
  on:click={clickFunction ?? (() => {})}
/>
```

### Importance

would make my life easier

title: Provide current value of store in second argument of stores
SSR-safe ID generation
body:
### Describe the problem

There are many cases where an application needs to connect DOM nodes with IDs:
* form fields and labels (`for`)
* accessible names (`aria-labelledby`)
* more [presented here](https://github.com/reactwg/react-18/discussions/111#discussioncomment-1517265)

Given that these IDs do not need any semantic meaning, and given that humans are pretty terrible at coming up with app-level unique IDs, this is a job wonderfully suited for a framework. Taking SSR into consideration, we cannot simply use counter-based solutions or randomly generated IDs.

### Describe the proposed solution

React 18 shipped its new [`useId()` hook](https://github.com/reactwg/react-18/discussions/111) which allows utilizing all the component tree knowledge of the framework and using that to generate IDs that are stable across SSR and unique across component instances.

I would like to see a similar thing in Svelte. It could look like this (`createInstanceId`):
```svelte
<!-- sign-in-form.svelte -->
<script lang="ts">
  import { createInstanceId } from 'svelte';
  
  const id = createInstanceId();
  const usernameID = `${id}-username`;
  const passwordID = `${id}-password`;
</script>

<label for={usernameID}>Username</label>
<input id={usernameID} />

<label for={passwordID}>Password</label>
<input id={passwordID} type="password" />
```

### Alternatives considered

#### Variable

The ID could come from a compiler-populated instance-specific variable:
```svelte
<label for={$$id}>Username</label>
<input id={$$id} />
```

Another name could be `$$instanceId`, to reflect its instance-dependency. This isn't perfect though, as it still doesn't communicate clearly enough that this isn't a component-specific variable, but rather an instance-specific one. A function call communicates that much better, similarly to `createEventDispatcher()`

#### Userland solution

I have used naive ID-generation solutions in the past (namely, [`lukeed/uid`](https://github.com/lukeed/uid)) and they didn't seem to cause any visible issues, but it's very likely that I simply haven't run into a use-case where a mismatch between the client and the server would be a problem.

Other userland solutions involve contexts, which is not great for developer experience, and might be problematic for asynchronous rendering (see https://github.com/reactwg/react-18/discussions/111#discussioncomment-1517189)

### Importance

would make my life easier

### Relevant mentions

https://github.com/sveltejs/svelte/issues/6932

title: Feature Suggestion: Improve versatility of `<svelte:component>` and `<svelte:element>` by treating them as a `<svelte:fragment>` when the `this` prop value is present but is a falsy or nullish value
body:
## Describe the problem

In some cases, I would like to conditionally render some content in a component or element.

## Describe the proposed solution

For these cases, it would be useful if we were able to conditionally omit the component or element by using a nullish or falsy value in the `this` prop. So this example (below) would simply render `Some text` since the `this` prop is a falsy value:

```svelte
<svelte:component this={false && MyComponent}>
  Some text
</svelte:component>
```

In such cases, the `<svelte:component>` or `<svelte:element>` would simply be treated as a `<svelte:fragment>`.

## Alternatives considered

The main alternative is see is similar but essentially creating my own `Fragment` component which simply returns the slotted content in this format:

```svelte
<slot {...$$restProps} />
```

In practice, it could be used like this:

```svelte
<svelte:component
  this={condition
    ? WrapperComponent
    : Fragment
  }
>
  Some text
</svelte:component>
```

The downside to this, aside from having to import another custom component is that it would not work at all for `<svelte:element>`. In those cases, I would actually have to create a Svelte component counterpart for every single element so I could use them against my new `Fragment` component like this:

```svelte
<script>
  import { Fragment, Div } from './customComponents.js';
  const condition = Math.random() < 0.5;
</script>

<svelte:component
  this={condition
    ? Div
    : Fragment
  }
>
  Some text
</svelte:component>
```

## Importance

would make my life easier

Some of my use cases: ```html ``` I've previously been using [Parcel](https://parceljs.org/), where I was able to add support for custom elements and attributes via a plugin. IMHO this deserves to be a built-in feature, as both web components and data-* attributes are well-established web standards. This issue has come up before (eg. https://github.com/vitejs/vite/issues/5098), but never really got addressed, as far as I can tell. The list of elements and attributes that Vite takes in as asset sources got extended over time (eg. https://github.com/vitejs/vite/pull/11138), but has remained a non-configurable constant. ### Suggested solution From skimming the code base, I get the impression that making [`DEFAULT_HTML_ASSET_SOURCES`](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/main/packages/vite/src/node/assetSource.ts#L41) a configurable option would handle my use cases. ### Alternative A plugin API to build DIY asset resolution would also work - just a function that one can stuff additional asset paths into should suffice. title: Add `envDir: false` option
body:
### Description

Currently, Dotenvx is not properly supported by Vite.

We are using [dotenvx](https://dotenvx.com/docs) (from the creator of dotenv) to manage our environment variables in Astro and Vite.
This means that a `.env` and a `.env.production` is available for every app in our monorepo with encrypted values, as follows:

SOME_ENV_VAR="encrypted:BA/01aCs2DHMHJc2SFeg...etcetc...f1TZg="

However, this currently results in Vite picking up the encrypted values without decrypting them. This results in unexpected situations, such as: running a production build with Astro as follows:
```bash
npx dotenvx run -f .env.production --strict -- astro build
```
I expect this command to only inject production .env values. However, Vite is automatically inserting the available `.env` file with encrypted values alongside the requested .env.production. This interferes with our Astro environment variable validation. We validate whether certain variables are present using Astro schema validation. Encrypted variables in the .env file are considered as "valid", even when encrypted (they are valid strings), therefore disrupting our env variable validation.

We currently use a workaround by setting the envDir to "bogus" in our Astro config. This is of course not a desirable solution.

Context @ Vite Discord: https://discord.com/channels/804011606160703521/1327200673518977046

Looking forward to work towards a solution together!

### Suggested solution

There are some directions:
- Adding an option to disable automatic .env-variable inclusion
- Adding a detection-mechanism for encrypted .env values
- ...

title: Add `module-sync` condition to default `ssr.resolve.externalCondition`
body:
### Description

[`module-sync` condition](https://nodejs.org/en/blog/release/v22.10.0#new-module-sync-exports-condition) is a condition enabled by Node.js when `require(esm)` is enabled. It is supported by the config loader (https://github.com/vitejs/vite/pull/18650), but not by the SSR module loader.

### Suggested solution

Add `module-sync` condition to default `ssr.resolve.externalCondition`.

### Alternative

Leave it as-is and tell users to configure it when needed.

### Additional context

- related: https://github.com/vitejs/vite/issues/18300
- we don't support `export { foo as 'module.exports' }` (https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/54563) in the config loader but we should support that as well
- The reason of not proposing adding `module-sync` to `ssr.resolve.conditions` is to follow Node.js's recommendation.
  Quoting from the Node 22.10.0 release post:
  > For **bundlers/tools**: they should avoid implementing this stop-gap condition. Most existing bundlers implement the de-facto bundler standard [**`module`**](https://webpack.js.org/guides/package-exports/#providing-commonjs-and-esm-version-stateless) exports condition, and that should be enough to support users who want to bundle ESM from CJS consumers. Users who want both bundlers and Node.js to recognize the ESM exports can use both **`module`**/**`module-sync`** conditions during the transition period, and can drop **`module-sync`**+**`module`** when they no longer need to support older versions of Node.js. If tools do want to support this condition, it's recommended to make the resolution rules in the graph pointed by this condition match the Node.js native ESM rules to avoid divergence.

title: Re-export PostCSS config type from `postcss-load-config`
body:
### Description

As a developer using Vite I want to be able to write type-safe PostCSS configs using the same version of `postcss-load-config` Vite uses so that I do not accidentally write configs that Vite cannot load correctly.

### Suggested solution

In Vite, we could re-export the type `postcssrc.Config` from `postcss-load-config` so that developers can use that type to write type-safe PostCSS configs.

### Alternative

- Not vendor `postcss-load-config` code (as suggested in https://github.com/vitejs/vite/issues/15869#issuecomment-1939414914)
- Writing PostCSS config inside Vite config
  - This only accepts the array format, and many examples use the object format; converting from the object format to the array format is not the most straightforward, especially if plugin options are involved
  - On a more subjective note, I prefer having each tool's config in a separate file, as it helps me mentally separate the context I need to consider
- Adding a devDependency on `postcss-load-config` per project to get access to the type in each project using PostCSS
  - This requires that all projects using Vite keep track of the version of `postcss-load-config` used by Vite to not use a wrong version and accidentally write a wrong config
- Not writing type-safe configs

### Additional context

Now that Vite 6 has updated `postcss-load-config` to v6, developers can now load TypeScript PostCSS config files easily, but ensuring that these configs are type-safe require us to add an additional dependency on `postcss-load-config`, which is less than ideal due to the possibility of a project's `postcss-load-config` differing from Vite's, which can lead to hard to debug errors.

body:
### Describe the bug

I'm migrating our angular projects from webpack to esbuild/vite, and ran into a problem with the vite proxy: Any non-synchronous calls in `proxy.bypass` result in errors, though they kinda work:

1. If I return a `Promise` from the bypass function, I get a compile or typing error:
```
error TS2322: Type '(req: IncomingMessage, res: ServerResponse<IncomingMessage>, proxyOptions: ProxyOptions) => false | Promise<...> | undefined' is not assignable to type '(req: IncomingMessage, res: ServerResponse<IncomingMessage>, options: ProxyOptions) => string | false | void | null | undefined'.
