title: Allow access to strict-mode JSON type coercions after JSON decode
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/get-started/) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

Context/Background:
Reported issue: https://github.com/psalvaggio/dynapydantic/issues/33
and the fix I came up with: https://github.com/psalvaggio/dynapydantic/pull/34

To distill the above context to a smaller reproducer:

```python
from pathlib import Path

from pydantic import BaseModel, TypeAdapter, ValidationError

class Model(BaseModel, strict=True):
    file_path: Path

adapter = TypeAdapter(Model)

decoded_json = {
    "file_path": "/tmp/example.txt",
}

# This is the value a field-level validator receives after
# model_validate_json() has decoded the JSON document.
try:
    adapter.validate_python(decoded_json, strict=True)
except ValidationError as exc:
    print("validate_python failed:")
    print(exc)

# Pydantic's JSON validation accepts the same string in strict mode
# and performs the JSON-specific Path coercion.
result = adapter.validate_json(
    '{"file_path": "/tmp/example.txt"}',
    strict=True,
)

print(result)
# Model(file_path=PosixPath('/tmp/example.txt'))
```

Given the constraints I have in my library, it would be desirable to be able to access the available type coercions in strict-mode JSON validation from the TypeAdapter. I could see this taking one of two forms:

1. Allow `strict` on `validate_python` to also take `"json_strict"` or something like that. This is appealing as a non-breaking API change.
2. Allow `validate_json` to take an already decoded object. This seems less desirable.

title: Allow arbitrary core schemas for serialization
body:
As per the TODO in https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/13487:

There is currently no way to tell `pydantic-core` "serialize this value using this core schema". `Ser`Schema is:

```python
SerSchema = Union[
    SimpleSerSchema,
    PlainSerializerFunctionSerSchema,
    WrapSerializerFunctionSerSchema,
    FormatSerSchema,
    ToStringSerSchema,
    ModelSerSchema,
]
```

The only member that expresses "use this schema" is `SimpleSerSchema`, and it does not take a schema at all, only a name from a closed literal:

```python
ExpectedSerializationTypes = Literal[
    'none', 'int', 'bool', 'float', 'str', 'bytes', 'bytearray', 'list', 'tuple',
    'set', 'frozenset', 'generator', 'dict', 'datetime', 'date', 'time', 'timedelta',
    'url', 'multi-host-url', 'json', 'uuid', 'any',
]

class SimpleSerSchema(TypedDict, total=False):
    type: Required[ExpectedSerializationTypes]
```

So an arbitrary schema (a model, a dataclass, `list[int]`, a TypedDict, anything constructed by the schema generator) cannot be used directly. Every place in Pydantic that needs it works around the gap the same way: it wraps the schema in a wrap serializer whose function is the identity, purely so the schema can ride along in the `schema` argument.

From `ValidateAs.__get_pydantic_core_schema__()`:

https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/27f95c789b20aa23306e5ce559327db0e9a10a6e/pydantic/functional_validators.py#L911-L917

title: Add Prototype() in the metadata's Annotated of a function attribute for TypeAdapter to use
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/get-started/) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

Hi,

My use case is in Fastmcp where i want my tool (python function) to accept incomplete BaseModel (missing fields, no model validation). The idea is to use the filled information as a search query and return to the llm all BaseModel that match. 

Fastmcp uses TypeAdapter for calling the function tool (validate_python) and also for getting the JSON schema (json_schema) that will be sent to the llm.

Consider the following example:

```python
from typing import Annotated, List, Union
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, Prototype # new Prototype class

class Car(BaseModel):
    owner: Annotated[str, Field()]
    color: Annotated[str, Field()]

class Bus(BaseModel):
    company: Annotated[str, Field()]
    color: Annotated[str, Field()]

vehicules: List[Union[Car, Bus]] = []

def get_vehicules(
    vehicule: Annotated[Union[Car, Bus], Prototype()],
):
    results = [found for found in vehicules if found.__class__ == vehicule._class__]
    for field in vehicule.__class__.model_fields:
        if hasattr(vehicule, field):
            for result in results:
                if getattr(result, field) != getattr(vehicule, field):  # will need a correct __eq__ for BaseModel fields
                    results.remove(result)
    return results

# adapter that knows that the vehicule attribute is a prototype because of Protoype()
adapter = TypeAdapter(get_vehicules)
# send the JSON Schema of get_vehicules to the llm, saying that Car and Bus BaseModel have all their required model fields accepting null values if their current type does not already accept null.
# Then if a field is required in the model, it is still required in the JSON Schema but the llm can put the field to null (this is for pydantic to differentiate a bus from a car)
adapter.json_schema()
# get the blue cars
search_result = adapter.validate_python({"vehicule": {"owner": None, "color": "blue"}})  # None is null in JSON
# get the blue buses
search_result = adapter.validate_python({"vehicule": {"company": None, "color": "blue"}})
``` 

Note: you may need first to support dictionary (python/json) for fields of type BaseModel in model_construct. Today it only supports BaseModel instance. See issue 8084.

title: BaseModel-like API for top-level discriminated unions
body:
### Description

This is related to #10409, especially the later comments asking whether `TypeAdapter` can behave more like a `BaseModel`.

Using the docs example:

```py
from typing import Annotated, Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, RootModel, TypeAdapter


class Cat(BaseModel):
    pet_type: Literal["cat"]
    meows: int


class Dog(BaseModel):
    pet_type: Literal["dog"]
    barks: float


class Lizard(BaseModel):
    pet_type: Literal["reptile", "lizard"]
    scales: bool


type Pet = Annotated[
    Cat | Dog | Lizard,
    Field(discriminator="pet_type"),
]
```

For a nested field, the documented pattern works well:

```py
class Model(BaseModel):
    pet: Pet
```

But for a flat top-level object, the available options all have tradeoffs:

```py
pet = TypeAdapter(Pet).validate_python({"pet_type": "cat", "meows": 3})
pet.pet_type  # works
pet.model_dump()  # works
```

But `TypeAdapter` itself is not model-like:

```py
TypeAdapter(Pet).model_validate(...)  # not available
```

`RootModel` gives a model-like API, but wraps the actual object under `.root`:

```py
class PetModel(RootModel[Pet]):
    pass

pet = PetModel.model_validate({"pet_type": "cat", "meows": 3})
pet.root.pet_type  # works
pet.pet_type       # does not
```

Is there, or should there be, a Pydantic-native way to define a top-level discriminated union that:

- preserves the flat input/output shape
- selects the correct concrete model using the discriminator
- is constructible/validatable like a `BaseModel`
- exposes the selected model's fields directly, without `.root`

In other words, something with the ergonomics of `TypeAdapter(Pet).validate_python(...)`, but with a first-class model-style API.

title: Add a global option to serialise/deserialise enums by name not value
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

There's an existing [discussion](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/discussions/2980) about this which started off as a feature request but was changed to a discussion. I think that discussion has run its course so I'd like to make a feature request which can either be progressed, or closed if the project does not want to go that way.

This feature request is for a single, global flag added to the configuration:

- Add a boolean configuration option: "serialise_enum_by_name" or similar, default False.
- If it is False: no change to serialisation / schemas.
- If it is True: serialisation / de-serialisation uses the enum name, and generated schemas contain a list of enum names.

I think this needs to be part of the core library as there have been a few suggested workarounds over time in the linked discussion, but they all rely on specific internal behaviour at the time and eventually break with newer releases.

There is some discussion in the linked issue of a non-global requirement that could be applied to specific enum instances. I'd like to explicitly exclude those from this feature request: I think that is a sufficiently different use case that if people want that it should go in its own request.

title: Ability to pass context to __get_pydantic_core_schema__ and __get_pydantic_json_schema__
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

I maintain the following library: https://github.com/psalvaggio/dynapydantic https://psalvaggio.github.io/dynapydantic/latest/

The general idea of the library is to offer polymorphic validation to mirror the polymorphic serialization that has been added to pydantic. Essentially, classes keep track of their children via `__pydantic_init_subclass__`, register them, the create unions to serve as field annotations.

Initially, I made this work with a custom annotation around the base class, but I have come up with a way to make the following syntax work:

```python
import dynapydantic
import pydantic

class Base(
    dynapydantic.SubclassTrackingModel,
    union_mode="smart",
    implicit_polymorphic=True,
):
    pass

class A(Base, extra="forbid"):
    a: int

class B(Base, extra="forbid"):
    other: Base

B(other={"other": {"other": {"a": 2}}}) # B(other=B(other=B(other=A(a=2))))
```

This requires overriding `__get_pydantic_core_schema__` and `__get_pydantic_json_schema__`, which works fine in the typical usage.

However, I'm running into issues with inheritance. Consider the following simple tree:

```python
Base <- Mid <- Leaf
```
If I put `Base` (let's pretend it is abstract) into my model, I'd want the field to accept `Mid` and `Leaf`, which are concrete. If I put `Mid` in there however, I'd want it to accept `Mid` or `Leaf`. Same thing if `Base` was not abstract and would be acceptable. This leads to two paths's to `__get_pydantic_core_schema__`:

1. If I use the type directly as a field annotation. Here I want to make the validator that validates the union.
2. If I am making a TypeAdapter from a base class's schema. Here I want the schema that would have been produced had I not overridden `__get_pydantic_core_schema__`.

However, I haven't been able to find a way to make this work. I've tried hacking around with patching the method away or using `contextvars`, but I think pydantic is caching the schema after the first call, which makes sense.

I think having a mechanism to pass context to `__get_pydantic_core_schema__` would allow me to make this all work, assuming the context itself was folded into the caching key.

Would this be a viable feature to add?

title: `model_copy(deep=True, update=...)` unnecessarily deepcopies fields that will be replaced by `update`
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

When calling `model_copy(deep=True, update={...})`, the current implementation deepcopies the **entire** model first, then applies the `update` dict afterwards:

```python
# pydantic/main.py
def model_copy(self, *, update=None, deep=False):
    copied = self.__deepcopy__() if deep else self.__copy__()  # full deepcopy first
    if update:
        ...
        copied.__dict__.update(update)  # then overwrite
    return copied
```

This means fields specified in `update` are deepcopied and then immediately discarded. This causes two problems:

1. **Wasteful performance**: fields that will be replaced are deepcopied for nothing.
2. **Fails on non-copyable fields**: if a field contains an object that cannot be deepcopied (e.g., native C extensions, file handles, GPU tensors), `model_copy` raises an error — even though the caller explicitly intends to replace that field via `update`.

### Example Code

```python
import mujoco
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict


class PhysicsEngine:
    """Wraps a native MuJoCo simulation (not deepcopy-safe)."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.model = mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_string("<mujoco/>")
        self.data = mujoco.MjData(self.model)


class AppConfig(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(arbitrary_types_allowed=True)

    name: str = "default"
    engine: PhysicsEngine = None


config = AppConfig(engine=PhysicsEngine())

# This FAILS even though we are replacing `engine`:
copy = config.model_copy(
    deep=True,
    update={"engine": None},  # explicitly replacing the non-copyable field
)
# ValueError: negative dimensions are not allowed
# (from deepcopy trying to copy the MuJoCo native structs)
```

### Proposed Solution

**Option A (minimal):** Add a parameter (e.g., `update_before_copy: bool = False`) to control the order of operations:

```python
def model_copy(self, *, update=None, deep=False, update_before_copy=False):
    if update_before_copy and update:
        # Apply update on a shallow copy first, then deepcopy
        shallow = self.__copy__()
        # apply update to shallow copy
        ...
        copied = shallow.__deepcopy__() if deep else shallow
    else:
        # Current behavior (backward compatible)
        copied = self.__deepcopy__() if deep else self.__copy__()
        if update:
            ...
    return copied
```

**Option B (better default):** When `deep=True` and `update` is provided, skip deepcopy for fields present in `update`. This is both more efficient and avoids the unnecessary failure:

```python
def model_copy(self, *, update=None, deep=False):
    if deep and update:
        # Shallow copy first, apply update, then deepcopy only the remaining fields
        copied = self.__copy__()
        copied.__dict__.update(update)
        for key, value in copied.__dict__.items():
            if key not in update:
                copied.__dict__[key] = deepcopy(value)
    elif deep:
        copied = self.__deepcopy__()
    else:
        copied = self.__copy__()
        if update:
            copied.__dict__.update(update)
    return copied
```

title: Support for x-enum-varnames (Enum member names) in JSON Schema Generator
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

Hi! Thanks for the great library!

I need support for the `x-enum-varnames` OpenAPI 3 extension field in the JSON Schema Generator and was curious to see whether there is interests in adding support directly to pydantic, rather than simply creating a custom generator.
I have implemented a [PR](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/13004), and would love to commit it if there is interest.

### Context

`x-enum-varnames` maintains the key(name) of any enum value that defines it in the form `name = 'value'`.
  The default behavior is to use the value as both the key and value.
  This is a frequently supported extension field in OpenAPI 3 and is used by many code generators to allow generating bot Python and Typescript enums in the following form:

```python
class Fruit(Enum):
    apple = 'Apple'
    grape = 'Grape'
``` 
```typescript
export enum Fruit {
    apple = "Apple",
    grape = "Grape"
}
``` 

Without this extension we lose this extra information, and a 1:1 recreation of the original code is impossible:
```python
class Fruit(Enum):
    Apple = 'Apple'
    Grape = 'Grape'
``` 

### Proof Of Concept
In my PR I have added a new option 

**`use_x_enum_varnames`**: `bool`
Default: `False`
```
Whether the generated json-schema/OpenAPI 3 enums should have the `x-enum-varnames` extension populated.
This maintains the key of any enum value that defines it in the form `key = 'value'`.
The default behavior is to use the value as both the key and value.
This is a frequently supported extension field in OpenAPI 3.
```

### Example

```python
from enum import Enum

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict

class SomeEnum(Enum):
    FOO = 'foo'
    BAR = 'bar'
    BAZ = 'baz'

class DefaultModel(BaseModel):
    value: SomeEnum

DefaultModel.model_json_schema()['$defs']['SomeEnum']
# "SomeEnum": {
#     "enum": ["foo", "bar", "baz"],
#     "title": "SomeEnum",
#     "type": "string"
# }

class VarnamesModel(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(use_x_enum_varnames=True)
    value: SomeEnum

VarnamesModel.model_json_schema()['$defs']['SomeEnum']
# {
#     'enum': ['foo', 'bar', 'baz'],
#     'title': 'SomeEnum',
#     'type': 'string',
#     'x-enum-varnames': ['FOO', 'BAR', 'BAZ'],
# }
```

title: `BaseModel.model_zip()` - construct a list of models from column-oriented data
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

A common pattern when working with Pydantic models is constructing a list of instances from parallel sequences - essentially a column-to-row transpose:

```python
orders = [
    Order(customer=c, product=p, quantity=q)
    for c, p, q in zip(customers, products, quantities, strict=True)
]
```

This comes up frequently in data processing pipelines, ETL code, and API layers where intermediate results are naturally columnar (one list per field) but the final output is a list of validated models.

**Proposed API**

A classmethod on `BaseModel`:

```python
orders = Order.model_zip(customer=customers, product=products, quantity=quantities)
```

Equivalent to the comprehension above, but:

- Validates that all sequences have the same length (raises on mismatch)
- Each row is validated through the normal model constructor

Of course, the name doesn't have to be `model_zip` :)

**Why this belongs in Pydantic**

`model_zip` would be a natural batched counterpart to normal model construction. Pydantic already provides field-aware tooling around model instantiation, including mypy plugin support and editor support in  e.g., VS Code. A built-in `BaseModel.model_zip(...)` would extend that experience to the common case where data is organized by field rather than by row.

Pydantic is also the right layer for this because it already owns the model’s field definitions and runtime validation semantics. While users can validate `list[MyModel]`, they still need to manually transpose columnar inputs first. `model_zip` would fill that gap with a small, explicit API for a common pattern.

**Alternatives considered**

- **Keep the comprehension**: Works, is type-safe (the IDE sees the constructor call), but verbose and repetitive when the pattern recurs across many call sites. This repetition is what brought me to write this request.
- **`TypeAdapter`**: Validates data against a type but has no columnar construction API.
- **`Unpack[TypedDict]`** (PEP 692): Could type specific kwargs, but AFAIK requires a separate TypedDict per model -- defeats the purpose of a generic utility. Unless I'm missing something?

body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything

### Description

If a pydantic base model allows extra fields, they get included in `model_dump` by default, e.g.
```python
class A(BaseModel, extra="allow"):
    a: int

a = A(a=1, b="test")
print(a)  # A(a=1, b='test')
print(a.model_dump())  # {'a': 1, 'b': 'test'}
```
There are cases where we might want to exclude the extra fields from being dumped. The requested feature being something like
```python
print(a.model_dump(exclude_extra=True))  # {'a': 1}
```
`exclude_extra` would be `False` by default preserving the current behaviour.

Technically, this can be done today by doing something like
```python
a_dict = a.model_dump()
for k in a.model_extra:
    a_dict.pop(k)
```
But this is cumbersome, especially if doing `model_dump_json` since you have to deserialize, remove extra fields and then reserialize the dict, which defeats the point of calling `model_dump_json`. Having the option to exclude the extra fields to begin with would be nice.

title: Stdlib dataclass custom docstrings suppressed from JSON schema description
body:
source https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/pull/4138#discussion_r2818450381

### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Pydantic suppresses `__doc__` from stdlib dataclasses in JSON schema generation to avoid auto-generated signature docstrings (e.g. `'Foo(x: int = 1)'`) leaking as `description`. However, the suppression doesn't distinguish between auto-generated and custom docstrings — explicit docstrings are also dropped.

This is inconsistent with Pydantic dataclasses, which DO get their custom docstrings included.

The suppression is in `GenerateJsonSchema.dataclass_schema` (`pydantic/json_schema.py`):

```python
if is_stdlib_dataclass(cls):
    # vanilla dataclass; don't use cls.__doc__ as it will contain the class signature by default
    description = None
```

And similarly in `_update_class_schema`:

```python
docstring = None if cls is BaseModel or dataclasses.is_dataclass(cls) else cls.__doc__
```

Python makes it straightforward to distinguish auto-generated from custom docstrings — the auto-generated ones start with `f'{cls.__name__}('`.

This became more visible after #11822 fixed `is_stdlib_dataclass` (previously `is_builtin_dataclass`), which had a bug where dataclasses with `KW_ONLY` sentinel annotations were not recognized as stdlib dataclasses and accidentally got their docstrings preserved.

### Example Code

```python
# /// script
# requires-python = '>=3.10'
# dependencies = [
#     'pydantic>=2.12',
# ]
# ///
import dataclasses

import pydantic
import pydantic.dataclasses
from pydantic import TypeAdapter


@dataclasses.dataclass
class StdlibNoDoc:
    x: int = 1


@dataclasses.dataclass
class StdlibWithDoc:
    """A custom docstring that should appear as 'description' in JSON schema."""

    x: int = 1


@pydantic.dataclasses.dataclass
class PydanticWithDoc:
    """A custom docstring that should appear as 'description' in JSON schema."""

    x: int = 1


print(f'pydantic=={pydantic.__version__}')
print()

for cls in [StdlibNoDoc, StdlibWithDoc, PydanticWithDoc]:
    schema = TypeAdapter(cls).json_schema()
    desc = schema.get('description')
    print(f'{cls.__name__}:')
    print(f'  __doc__     = {cls.__doc__!r}')
    print(f'  description = {desc!r}')
    print()
```

### Output

```
pydantic==2.12.5

StdlibNoDoc:
  __doc__     = 'StdlibNoDoc(x: int = 1)'
  description = None

StdlibWithDoc:
  __doc__     = "A custom docstring that should appear as 'description' in JSON schema."
  description = None

PydanticWithDoc:
  __doc__     = "A custom docstring that should appear as 'description' in JSON schema."
  description = "A custom docstring that should appear as 'description' in JSON schema."
```

**Expected**: `StdlibWithDoc` should also have `description` set since it has an explicit custom docstring.

platform: macOS

title: Extract type arguments used to specialize generic models at run-time
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

I've been working on porting a Pydantic V1 [application](https://salsa.debian.org/freexian-team/debusine) to V2, and in the process found myself needing to import from `pydantic._internal._generics`.  Neither my reviewer nor I can think of a better way to do things at the moment, but we agreed it would make sense to file an issue upstream.

A number of parts of our database schema are structured with a category field and some JSON data fields; the category field selects the schema used to parse the JSON data fields.  For example, we have several different kinds of "artifact", each of which has its own schema for "artifact data".  The code to handle each artifact of course wants to work with a validated Pydantic model instance rather than the raw JSON data, but we wanted to keep things reasonably DRY by not repeating the code needed to construct the model in lots of different places.

I invented a pattern that we've found to work well across our application.  When ported to Pydantic V2, it looks something like this (reduced):

```python
import abc
import enum
from types import GenericAlias
from typing import Any, ClassVar, Generic, TypeVar, cast

import pydantic
from pydantic._internal._generics import get_args, get_origin


# The return type is really typing._GenericAlias, but that's private.
def _get_specialization(cls: type, base: type) -> Any:
    """
    Inspect a class for its specialization of a generic base class.

    A class may specialize a generic base class in various ways: for
    example, it might supply specific values for some of the relevant type
    variables, or it might itself be generic and rely on being specialized
    by its own subclasses, or both.  To help us introspect such classes,
    this returns the specialization of `base` by `cls` in the form of a
    :py:class:`typing._GenericAlias`.

    :raises AssertionError: if `cls` specializes `base` in different ways by
      means of multiple inheritance.
    """
    specializations: set[GenericAlias] = set()
    if hasattr(cls, "__pydantic_generic_metadata__"):
        orig_bases = [get_origin(cls)[get_args(cls)]]
    else:
        orig_bases = getattr(cls, "__orig_bases__", [])
    for cls_base in orig_bases:
        origin = get_origin(cls_base)
        if origin == base:
            specializations.add(cls_base)
        elif origin is not None and issubclass(origin, base):
            specializations.add(
                _get_specialization(origin, base)[get_args(cls_base)]
            )
    if len(specializations) != 1:
        raise AssertionError(
            f"{cls.__qualname__} must specialize {base.__qualname__} with "
            f"exactly one consistent list of type arguments "
            f"(got {specializations})"
        )
    [specialization] = specializations
    return specialization


def extract_generic_type_arguments(
    cls: type, expected_origin: type
) -> tuple[type, ...]:
    """
    Extract type arguments from a generic class.

    This is expected to be called from __init_subclass__ in a generic class
    (i.e. one that has Generic[...] as a base class), and allows extracting
    the specializing type arguments so that they can be used as factories.
    """
    args = get_args(_get_specialization(cls, expected_origin))
    assert isinstance(args, tuple)
    return args

    SOURCE_PACKAGE = "debian:source-package"

class DebianSourcePackage(ArtifactData):
    name: str
    version: str
    dsc_fields: dict[str, Any]


AD = TypeVar("AD", bound=ArtifactData)

body:
### Initial Checks

### Description

When something else (and not the `ImportString` import path) produces an `ImportError`, `ImportString`'s error handling catches the exception and assumes it has been produced by the user-provided import path. 

This results in a misleading and confusing exception message. 

### Example Code

```py

from pydantic.types import ImportString

adapter: TypeAdapter[type] = TypeAdapter(ImportString)

# This import path points to a valid module, but that module has its own ImportError
import_path = "my_module.MyClass"

print("Attempting to validate import path:", import_path)
print()

# What Pydantic reports:
print("=== Pydantic ImportString error ===")
try:
    adapter.validate_python(import_path)
except Exception as e:
    print(f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}")

print()

# What the actual error is:
print("=== Actual ImportError ===")
try:
    import my_module
except ImportError as e:
    print(f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}")
```

### Initial Checks

### Description

I would like to propose adding a built in `Port` type, similar in spirit to existing network types.

When handling configuration, network ports can be very common. It would be ideal if, when parsing such configuration, ports could be represented in a type safe and semantically meaningful way.

Ports have a clear meaning, and while it can be argued that ports are simply integers with a defined range, this semantic information is currently lost in most model definitions.

Currently, a way to solve the issue with having a typesafe `Port` could be the following:

```python
Port = Annotated[int, Field(ge=0, le=65535)]

class SomeConfig(BaseModel):
    port: Port
```

While the above example works, it leads to each project needing to define its own type. I believe implementing `Port` can provide a more centralized and reusable definition. It could also raise the intuition that a port also needs to be validated and not simply be taken as is, and applications would be able to fail at an earlier stage.

title: Premature warning about Python 3.14 in pydantic.v1
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

When a module is imported `from pydantic.v1` and a user is running Python 3.14, they'll get a warning: "Core Pydantic V1 functionality isn't compatible with Python 3.14 or greater."

On the surface, the logic here is sound: if the user is importing something from `pydantic.v1` they must be about to use that thing, so let's warn them that it's not going to work.

But there are packages that import classes from V1 just to _check_ if the end user is using V1. For example, [LangChain in this file](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain/blob/master/libs/core/langchain_core/utils/pydantic.py).

In these cases, the warning is confusing and sends developers down a rabbit hole of trying to work out "who's trying to use Pydantic V1?" and if they don't know Python intimately, they might think that different packages are using different versions of Pydantic at the same time and they're clashing, all rather unpleasant, considering that nothing's actually wrong!

I see three possible futures:
1. Python 3.14 users in this situation get warnings, they can ignore them (warning fatigue, not great)
2. All packages that do this "import from `pydantic.v1` to check usage" pattern fix their code to check in some way that doesn't involve importing from `pydantic.v1` (probably not going to happen)
3. Pydantic refines the logic to only show this warning when it looks like something is actually going to break (e.g. triggered in the constructors of classes)

The current logic is going to be helpful to a shrinking number of users, and rather annoying for a growing number of users.

Relevant PR: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/12263

title: [Request] Built-in validation of lists and dicts of BaseModels (e.g. via RootModel children)
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

Suppose I have a simple model:

```python

from pydantic import BaseModel

Foo(BaseModel):
    bar: str
```
I might have an external data source that will sometimes return a `Foo`, but other times it might return a `list[Foo]` or `dict[something, Foo]`. How do you validate this? A naive approach might be `[Foo.model_validate(foo) for foo in response]`. This often works, but what if `response` is not a `list`? Or it's a `dict` instead (in which case you're inadvertently making a list of the keys).

It's very convenient to have pydantic handle all of these edge cases for you. One way is another `BaseModel` child with a `list[Foo]` attribute. Another way is by using `RootModel`. This is nice because it also lets you take advantage of `Protocol` to automatically call `model_validate` on arbitraily-typed responses from your external data sources. If for some reason, though, you need the post-validation object to be used directly (e.g. 3rd party library), then having to carry around the `.root` makes this break.

What we end up doing in our libraries is something like this:

```python
_V = TypeVar("_V", bound=BaseModel)

class ListModel(RootModel[list[_V]]):
    def append(self, value: _V):
        self.root.append(value)

    def extend(self, values: Iterable[_V]) -> None:
        self.root.extend(values)

    def insert(self, index: SupportsIndex, value: _V) -> None:
        self.root.insert(index, value)

    # And so on; whatever other methods we need.
```

You can do something similar with `dict`.

It would be great if something to handle these types of scenarios were built into pydantic to enable something like these:
```python
from pydantic import ListModel

class ListOfFoo(ListModel[Foo]):
    pass

ListOfFoo.model_validate(data)

Baz = ListModel[Foo]

baz = Baz.model_validate(response)
baz[0]
baz.pop()
# etc
```

I'm not convinced our approach is the best one, but I haven't come across anything else that's wildly better. Another possibility we considered was something like:
```
from pydantic import ListOf

result: list[Foo] = ListOf(Foo).model_validate(response)
```
It's nice to return the list directly rather than have it wrapped in a subclass, but there were too many edge cases to worry about.

---
I'm creating this both to open a discussion on the topic and also to offer to help in development.

### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

It can sometimes be useful to treat validation errors coming the same model differently, based on the place in the code, where the validation was attempted.

One particular use case for this is a web application, which puts data fetched from a database into a model instance. `ValidationError` raised here should be considered a server-side error and treated differently from failing to validate a request body (which is a client-side error).

One way to differentiate validation failures is to allow setting an exception class or instance to be re-raised from a `ValidationError`, i.e.:

```python
class Model(BaseModel):
    # `model_config` can contain an optional exception class to be used by default for `Model`
    model_config = ConfigDict(custom_validation_exception=SomeException)
```

```python
def model_validate(
    ...
    # An override for the specific `model_validate` call, which has the priority
    # over `model_config` exception, if set, and could be provided with `ValidationError`
    # to disable re-raising
    custom_validation_exception: Exception | type[Exception] | None = None
):
    ...
    # `CustomExceptionContextManager` catches `ValidationError` and re-raises `exc` from it,
    # if `exc` is not resolved to None or `ValidationError`
    exc = custom_validation_exception or cls.model_config.get("custom_validation_exception")
    with CustomExceptionContextManager(exc):
        return cls.__pydantic_validator__.validate_python(
        ...
        )
```

Another potential option is to restrict both `custom_validation_exception` values to `ValidationError` and its subclasses and use them directly in pydantic-core (although I can't properly assess the possibility & the amount of work required to do so).

It's certainly possible to add similar exception handling on the side of a library user, however a Pydantic implementation of this feature -- at least for the `model_validate` & `model_validate_json` methods -- seems to be less verbose and should not introduce any breaking changes.

### Description

Currently,even if a type can be converted, the type-checker/linter will show an error
```python
class Number(BaseModel):
   value: int

   @model_validator(mode="before")
   @classmethod
   def _from_string(cls, value):

class Number(BaseModel):

   @classmethod
   def _from_string(cls, value):
        if isinstance(value, dict):
            return value
        return {"value": value}

class User(BaseModel):

title: Allow documenting custom type aliases via typing_extensions.Doc
Preserve `NamedTuple` class during validation
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

This is what I'm observing:

```Python
import pydantic
from typing import NamedTuple


class A(NamedTuple):
    x: int


class B(NamedTuple):
    x: int


class C(pydantic.BaseModel):
    a_or_b: A | B


c = C(a_or_b=B(x=1))
print(c)

# expected: a_or_b=B(x=1)
# prints: a_or_b=A(x=1)
```

This short-circuits on type arguments in the union in order in the `smart` mode of unions (`left_to_right` I assume makes no difference, the problem lies in exactness).
If we reverse it, the output will show `B` because `B` was first that structurally matched.

It works this way in strict mode too.
This resembles `left_to_right` more than `smart` mode of the union schema.

Conceptually, Pydantic looks for ways to match namedtuple as a structural type, whereas the nominal bit was missed.

This applies to old-fashion named tuples as well:
```py
from collections import namedtuple

import pydantic

A = namedtuple('A', 'x')
B = namedtuple('B', 'x')

class C(pydantic.BaseModel):
    a_or_b: A | B

c = C(a_or_b=B(x=1))
print(c)  # a_or_b=A(x=1)
```

We would want to convert between uniform namedtuples in non-strict mode -- sure:

```py
import pydantic
from typing import NamedTuple


class A(NamedTuple):
    x: int


class B(NamedTuple):
    x: int


class C(pydantic.BaseModel):
    only_a: A


c = C(only_a=B(x=1))
print(c)  # only_a=A(x=1)
```

but I'm not so sure we want the union schema to miss the nominal type of the input. If we can preserve the original type, my instinct is that we'd want to keep it. Esp. since we don't observe this behavior with dataclasses (namedtuples are of quite different nature, though).

The current behavior can be interpreted as a feature, not a bug -- feel free to relabel this as a feature request if you do think that's true.

## In short

I'm proposing a feature to, in validation, validate every namedtuple input against its targeted namedtuple class (so, `return_schema` -- seems like `return_schema` isn't used by namedtuple schemas yet) **before** proceeding with the call validator logic and deconstructing it as a collection of arguments and trying a call to the namedtuple constructor. It would be based on a new `idempotent` flag in `CallValidator` -- if a function call is idempotent, the validation should start from the return validator -- if that doesn't pass, only then try to call. As a result, nominal types wouldn't be swapped in unions of namedtuples in smart union mode.

Do you guys think this is worth adding to pydantic, or too much hassle for an edge case?
Thanks!

PS One more thing. This relies on the assumption that instance checks guarantees type safety of the object's state.

If the namedtuple instance contains unsound data, its internals wouldn't be re-validated and fixed up in place as it happens right now. In this sense, the change could be breaking. 

The same that would happen here already happens for dataclasses in Pydantic:

```py
from dataclasses import dataclass

from pydantic import BaseModel


@dataclass
class Foo:
    x: int


malformed = Foo(x="1")

class Model(BaseModel):
    foo: Foo

print(Model(foo=malformed))
```

If someone has an unsure instance of a namedtuple, they would need to re-validate it through type adapter, perhaps.
Or just use models directly on raw data -- for 99.999% of people this won't happen.

title: Docstrings leaking into JSON Schema descriptions impact agentic production systems
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

In Pydantic v2, a model’s class docstring automatically becomes the "description" field in the generated JSON Schema. This is convenient for documentation, but it implicitly makes comments part of the runtime contract because many runtimes (especially LLM and agent frameworks) now consume those schemas directly to decide behavior.

A harmless docstring edit can change tool selection or behavior in production.

This coupling is amplified because LLM platforms explicitly encourage Pydantic for structured output/tool schemas (ie [OpenAI](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/structured-outputs) and I believe PydanticAI has same risk although I haven't had the time to experiment there yet).

Developers don’t expect docstrings to affect runtime behaviour.
The software folklore tale [The Inner JSON Effect](https://thedailywtf.com/articles/the-inner-json-effect) illustrates how comments bleeding into contracts can become a subtle foot-gun.


LLM agents often read schema "description"s to decide which tool/model to use; a teammate “polishing” a docstring can alter production outcomes.
On top of that, docstrings are frequently edited without the same review rigor as public contracts.


### Example Code

```Python
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Foo(BaseModel):
    """An example base model"""
    pass


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(Foo.model_json_schema())

# > {'description': 'An example base model', 'properties': {}, 'title': 'Foo', 'type': 'object'}
```

title: Add utility function to convert Pydantic model fields to dictionary representation for API documentation
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description


## Summary
Add a utility function that converts Pydantic model fields to a human-readable dictionary representation, particularly useful for generating API documentation and Swagger/OpenAPI schemas.

## Motivation
When building APIs with Pydantic models, developers often need to programmatically generate documentation that shows the expected structure of request/response bodies. Currently, there's no built-in way to convert a Pydantic model field structure into a clean, readable dictionary format that can be easily used for:

- Auto-generating API documentation
- Creating Swagger/OpenAPI schema descriptions
- Providing clear examples in API responses
- Debugging and development tools

## Proposed Solution
A new utility function `pydantic_model_to_dict()` that would:

1. **Handle nested models**: Recursively process Pydantic models within models
2. **Support primitive types**: Convert basic Python types (int, str, float, etc.) to readable names
3. **Handle Optional types**: Properly format `Union[Type, None]` as `Optional[Type]`
4. **Support Union types**: Format multiple type unions as `[type1, type2]`
5. **Handle collections**: Format `List` and `Dict` types with their contained types
6. **Support Enums**: Display enum values as readable options

## Example Usage
```python
from pydantic import BaseModel
from typing import Optional, List, Dict
from enum import Enum

class Status(Enum):
    ACTIVE = "active"
    INACTIVE = "inactive"

class User(BaseModel):
    name: str
    age: Optional[int]
    status: Status
    tags: List[str]
    metadata: Dict[str, str]

# Would output something like:
# {
#   "name": "str",
#   "age": "Optional[int]", 
#   "status": "<active, inactive>",
#   "tags": "List[str]",
#   "metadata": "Dict[str, str]"
# }
```

## Benefits
- Improves developer experience when building APIs
- Reduces boilerplate code for documentation generation
- Provides consistent formatting across different projects
- Enhances debugging capabilities for complex model structures

## Implementation Considerations
- Should handle all current Pydantic field types
- Needs proper error handling for unsupported types
- Should maintain performance for large, deeply nested models
- Could be placed in `pydantic.utils` or similar module

Would this be a valuable addition to the Pydantic library? I've already done an implementation in local.

title: ENH: Add DataFrame.headtail() to show first and last N rows together
body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

## Problem Description

When inspecting a large DataFrame, it's common to want a quick look at both the beginning and the end of the data at the same time — for example, to sanity-check that a sort, concat, or time-series load looks correct from start to finish. Currently this requires calling `df.head()` and `df.tail()` separately and manually comparing the two outputs, which is a bit clunky, especially in notebooks where each call produces a separate output block.

### Feature Description

## Feature Description

Add a new method, e.g. `DataFrame.headtail(n=5)`, that returns a single DataFrame combining the first `n` and last `n` rows, similar to what `pd.concat([df.head(n), df.tail(n)])` would produce, but as a built-in convenience method. Ideally it would also insert a visual separator (similar to how `describe()` or truncated display uses `...`) to make clear that the middle rows are omitted, rather than implying the rows are contiguous.

Example usage:

```python
df.headtail(5)
```

Possible output:

```
   col1  col2
0     1     a
1     2     b
2     3     c
3     4     d
4     5     e
..  ...   ...
95   96     f
96   97     g
97   98     h
98   99     i
99  100     j
```

### Alternative Solutions

## Alternative Solutions

- Users can already do `pd.concat([df.head(n), df.tail(n)])`, but this doesn't include a visual separator and requires an extra import/call pattern.
- `pd.set_option('display.max_rows', 10)` combined with printing the full DataFrame gives a similar truncated view, but it changes global display state rather than returning a usable object, and doesn't work well outside of print/repr.

### Additional Context

## Additional Context

This would mainly be a display/inspection convenience method, similar in spirit to `head()`/`tail()`/`sample()`, useful for quick EDA on large DataFrames in notebooks and scripts.

title: ENH: Disclose offending values in `IntervalArray._validate`
body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

When using `IntervalIndex.from_breaks` one ends up at `IntervalArray._validate` which, among others asserts that the left end of the interval is `<=` to the right end.

Yet, it does not disclose the offending values and just raises a generic `left side of interval must be <= right side` `ValueError`. The provided values for the `IntervalArray` may be long so the user may not be able to easily spot the offenders.

### Feature Description

At this point an `Exception` is raised so one can assume the the library has completed its task. Hence a slight overhead for a improved error message may be acceptable. Only challenge is to not overcharge the error message, in case there are many offenders.

One possible solution could be to change

```python
        if not (left[left_mask] <= right[left_mask]).all():
            msg = "left side of interval must be <= right side"
```

to something like (pseudo code)

```python
order_offenders = left[left_mask] > right[left_mask]
if order_offenders.any():
    msg = f"left side of interval must be <= right side. offending intervals: {zip(left[order_offenders], right[order_offenders]}"
```

### Alternative Solutions

Alternatively, if this seems to risky or resource intensive, maybe just printing the first 5 offending indices is already helpful

(pseudocode)

```python
order_offenders = left[left_mask] > right[left_mask]
if order_offenders.any():
    msg = f"left side of interval must be <= right side. offending locations: {order_offenders[order_offenders].index.head(5)}"
```

### Additional Context

_No response_

title: ENH: Add limit_distance parameter to Series/DataFrame.interpolate
body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

I wish I could use pandas' interpolate method such that I could pass a parameter 'limit_distance' which will make it so that when two values differ by more than limit_distance, pandas will not interpolate.

I think this is similar to how the existing limit parameter works to prevent interpolation when there are too many NaNs in between, but instead of counting missing values, it prevents interpolation if the actual coordinate or time gap between two valid points is too big.

I encountered this issue while trying to work on ECG data and was instructed not to interpolate over long gaps, I realized that the most efficient way is not to interpolate conditionally, but rather to interpolate and then filter (remove unwanted interpolations); I think this is due to CPu and cache optimization but I am deviating from the main topic, I had to write code to do it and I thought that this could be cleaner to have this feature built in pandas.

Also, I think this may be related to issue #64588, which discusses limiting by consecutive NaN count, but this feature request specifically targets limiting by the actual numerical distance or time gap between anchor points rather than the number of missing cells.)

### Feature Description

I already implemented and tested this functionality locally. Here is the core helper method handling the vectorized gap logic:

```python
def _interp_limit_distance(
    indices: np.ndarray,
    invalid: npt.NDArray[np.bool_],
    limit_distance: float | int | str | Timedelta,
    unit: str | None = None,
) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Return index positions of invalid values that should not be filled
    because the x-axis distance between the surrounding valid points
    exceeds limit_distance.
    """
    # Normalize and validate limit_distance
    if isinstance(limit_distance, (str, Timedelta)):
        from pandas.core.tools.timedeltas import to_timedelta

        td = to_timedelta(limit_distance)
        if unit is not None:
            # Cast to matching NumPy timedelta unit ('s', 'ms', 'us', 'ns') then to int64
            threshold = td.to_numpy().astype(f"m8[{unit}]").astype(np.int64)
        else:
            threshold = td.value
    else:
        threshold = limit_distance

    if threshold <= 0:
        raise ValueError("limit_distance must be greater than 0")

    # Identify valid and invalid positions
    valid_pos = np.flatnonzero(~invalid)
    invalid_pos = np.flatnonzero(invalid)

    # everything is valid if there are less than 2 valid points
    # or if there are no NaNs (impossible/no need to interpolate)
    if len(valid_pos) < 2 or len(invalid_pos) == 0:
        return np.array([], dtype=np.int64)

    # For every NaN position, find the valid index immediately next to it
    right_idx = np.searchsorted(valid_pos, invalid_pos, side="left")

    # Only inspect NaNs that sit between two valid points (not leading/trailing NaNs)
    inside_mask = (right_idx > 0) & (right_idx < len(valid_pos))
    if not inside_mask.any():
        return np.array([], dtype=np.int64)

    # Map each interior NaN to its own array index and the array indexes
    # of the valid anchor points immediately to its left and right
    invalid_inside = invalid_pos[inside_mask]
    right_valid_pos = valid_pos[right_idx[inside_mask]]
    left_valid_pos = valid_pos[right_idx[inside_mask] - 1]

    # Calculate the physical x-axis gap across each NaN
    gap_sizes = np.abs(indices[right_valid_pos] - indices[left_valid_pos])

    if gap_sizes.dtype.kind in "mM":
        gap_sizes = gap_sizes.view("i8")

    # Return only the NaN positions where the gap exceeds the threshold
    return invalid_inside[gap_sizes > threshold]

title: ENH: UnicodeDecodeError from read_csv could suggest common alternative encodings
body:
### Feature Type

- [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

I wish read_csv's UnicodeDecodeError gave me a hint about what to try next, instead of just failing with no direction.

When read_csv hits a UnicodeDecodeError (e.g. a Windows Excel export saved as cp1252), the error gives no indication that trying a different encoding is the likely fix.

Reproducible example (pandas 3.0.2):

with open('test.csv', 'wb') as f:
    f.write(b'name,note\n')
    f.write(b'test,em' + bytes([0x97]) + b'dash\n')  # valid cp1252, invalid utf-8

import pandas as pd
pd.read_csv('test.csv')

Result:
UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0x97 in position 17: invalid start byte

This is a very common situation, Windows Excel commonly exports CSVs as cp1252, not utf-8, and the fix is almost always trying encoding='latin-1' or encoding='cp1252'. But nothing in the error message points there, so new users often don't realize encoding is even the problem.

### Feature Description

Append a short hint to the UnicodeDecodeError raised during CSV parsing when the default utf-8 encoding fails and the user hasn't explicitly set encoding.

Rough approach, in the CSV reading error handling path:

try:
    ...read with utf-8...
except UnicodeDecodeError as e:
    if encoding_was_default:
        raise UnicodeDecodeError(
            e.encoding, e.object, e.start, e.end,
            e.reason + ". Tip: this file may not be UTF-8 encoded. "
            "Try encoding='latin-1' or encoding='cp1252', common with Windows Excel exports."
        ) from e
    raise

This only changes the message text, not behavior, and only fires when encoding wasn't explicitly passed by the user, so it doesn't affect anyone who already specifies an encoding.

### Alternative Solutions

Currently the only options are:

1. Manually try common encodings one by one (utf-8, latin-1, cp1252) until one works, usually after searching Stack Overflow to learn this is the fix
2. Use a third-party library like chardet or charset-normalizer to detect the encoding beforehand, which is a heavier dependency for a one-line hint
3. Open the file in a text editor that reports encoding, then pass it explicitly

None of these are discoverable from the error message itself, which is the actual gap this request addresses.

### Additional Context

This is intentionally scoped narrower than a full encoding='detect' feature, since I understand that's a bigger design discussion. This is just improving the existing error message text for the common case.

title: ENH: Support %N directive in strptime parsing (to_datetime / Timestamp with format=)
body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

### Problem Description

GH-29461 / PR GH-64899 added a `%N` directive to `Timestamp.strftime` and the
array-level `strftime`, formatting nanoseconds as a 9-digit zero-padded number.
The parsing side does not accept it, so `%N` output doesn't round-trip with the
same format string:

```python
>>> ts = pd.Timestamp("2020-03-14 15:32:52.192548651")
>>> fmt = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%N"
>>> pd.to_datetime(ts.strftime(fmt), format=fmt)
ValueError: 'N' is a bad directive in format '%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%N'
```

Note that pandas' strptime already parses nanoseconds via `%f` (it accepts 1-9
digits, an extension over the stdlib's 6), so this is about symmetry and
round-tripping rather than new capability. Suggested in
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/64899#pullrequestreview-4481273478.

### Feature Description

Accept `%N` in `format=` for `to_datetime`, `Timestamp`, and related parsing
paths, matching exactly 9 digits (vs `%f`'s 1-9). Likely just an entry next to
`"f"` in the `TimeRE` class and corresponding handling in `strptime.pyx`.

### Alternative Solutions

Keep parsing via `%f`, which already handles 9 digits — but then a format
string built for `%N` output can't be reused for parsing.

### Additional Context

`Period.strftime` has long supported `%n`/`%N` for formatting only; linux
`date` uses `%N` for nanoseconds.

title: Add config option security.http.proxyFromEnvironment = false
body:
This is a security hardening issue.

In d6e6f9e500eebdeae8e28de830fff2e3bfc7d534 (unreleased) we added a dial-time URL validation.

If proxied (e.g. `HTTPS_PROXY` set on users machine or in CI) the above validation will only see the proxy address. There's no workaround for that, but I suggest by adding a new `security.http.proxyFromEnvironment` bool config flag (default disabled).

Thanks to @Reload3d for reporting this issue.

title: Improve/document security.http.urls override behavior
body:
In d6e6f9e500eebdeae8e28de830fff2e3bfc7d534 (unreleased) we added a dial-time URL validation to catch URLs that's valid according to the whitelist but that resolves to a loopback, private or link-local IP addresses. That check is skipped it if the user has a custom `security.http.urls` setup, as it would not make sense to block local development servers.

See `CheckAllowedHTTPAddress`.

This has been reported by @Reload3d  as a potential security issue, and while I think the current behaviour is the pragmatic correct approach, I'm creating this issue for visibility and to see if this can be improved further (e.g. better documentation).

title: Improve the return keyword in templates
body:
There's a long-living upstream issue about this (https://github.com/golang/go/issues/53015) which I don't think is going to be fixed in Go anytime soon.

We do have some patches to Go's template execution package, so if the fix I have in mind for this isn't too intrusive in that package (as in: it makes it very hard to maintain the fork), I think it's worth to improve this situation.

We have added a `return` keyword, but it currently have some limiations:

* It only works in partials.
* It must be the last command in the template.
* The current implementation, with its template transformations, has some complexities that would be great to rid of.

I have often wanted to return early, even from regular templates, which often avoids wrapping large block of templates in conditionals.

So, I suggest we have a look if it's feasible to introduce a sentinel error with an optional value (used in partials), so the template func (with the `return` alias) would be something ala:

```go
func (ns *Namespace) Return(args ...any) ReturnErr {
  var val any = nil
   if len(args) > 0 {
      val = args[0]
   }
   return &ReturnErr(val: val}}
}
```

And then somehow trapped in the template execution.

title: Remove tailwindcss from the default security.exec.allow list
body:
We enabled Node.js [permission model](https://nodejs.org/api/permissions.html#permission-model) in Hugo v0.161.0. This hardened the security for most of the JS tools that we support (e.g. PostCSS). Unfortunately, TailwindCSS needs a very [permissive setup](https://github.com/tailwindlabs/tailwindcss/discussions/20398) to run. Our [runtime security model](https://gohugo.io/about/security/#runtime-security) calls for pragmatic, but strict defaults. With that in mind, we need to remove `tailwindcss` from the default [allow list](https://gohugo.io/configuration/security/#execallow).

Note that you can easily re-add this to your `hugo.toml`, e.g:

```toml
  [security.exec]
    allow = ['^((dart-)?sass|go|npx|babel|node|git|postcss|tailwindcss)$']
```

Note that TailwindCSS is perfectly safe to use if you own/trust your theme to now do harmful things.

title: Make .Render take additional data

See https://gohugo.io/methods/page/render/#article
See #15076

> PAGE.Render NAME

This has been discussed before. 

* The contract has always been that the templates that `.Renders` gets the data context as e.g. `page.html`, a `page.Page`.
* We can only pass 1 argument to Go's template renderer, which I guess is the blocking reason for not having done this sooner.

So, if we want to do:

> PAGE.Render [DATA] NAME

I'm guessing we have 2 top-level options:

* We say that if `DATA` is set, we use that as the context passed to the templates,. else `PAGE`.
* We somehow (e.g. by embeding it in a `{ DataAdditionalContext, Page }` struct or  putting it into the current `context.Context`) wrap the `Page` so you can do both `.RelPermalink` and `.DataAdditionalContext` (naming of the latter is just picked out of a hat without thinking too hard.

I suggest we add `crypto.Fingerprint` with a similar signature to https://gohugo.io/functions/resources/fingerprint/

>hash.Fingerprint [ALGORITHM] any -> string

The purpose of such a construct is to organize content views in a dedicated directory.

title: Only support the latest Go version
body:
We currently hava N + N-1 Go version policy in Hugo. There are some growing pains maintaining this policy, which I don't remember exactly remember the origin reason for (I don't need it). I list some of the pain points below:

* `go mod init` defaults to the latest when writing the `go.mod`; that means that any new library written from start cannot be used by Hugo out of the box, and when one of the existing dependencies bumps their Go version in `go.mod`, we have a breakage and I have to [ask nicely](https://github.com/alecthomas/chroma/issues/1276) for them to adjust.
* We have a "soft fork" of Go's template packages, and syncing them after a new Go version often means manually rewrite new language constructs to old one to make it build on both.
* We need to run lengthy CI builds/tests on both versions x number of platforms.
* We need to wait until the next Go release before we can use any new Go feature.

Also, this is about the version needed to _build Hugo from source_, the release binaries will still work fine on PCs with no Go or older Go installed.

There may be some blocking reasons as to why we cannot do this, which is why I'm creating this issue so people can shout.

title: js: Resolve package names to module.esm.js in assets if found
body:
I'm doing some work automating and improving the harness around using NPM packages as Hugo Modules. And taking AlpineJS as an example:

It defines `"module": "dist/module.esm.js"` in `package.json`.

Assuming we mount that `dist` folder into `assets/alpinejs` we currently need to do:

```js
import Alpine from 'alpinejs/module.esm.js';
```

While the natural way and how most examples are set up is:

```js
import Alpine from 'alpinejs';
```

ESBuild's resolver (which we hand it over to when we fail to resolve in `assets`) are smarter about this and is reading `package.json` etc. to do the right thing.

I don't want to go down that route and complicate things to fix this, but I think it should be possible to expand `ResolveComponent` to also test the `module.esm.js` filename for these "package imports" (which I guess are paths without any slash?).

title: imaging: Add quality setting per image format
body:
The current default is 75 for all the formats that support it (JPEG, WebP and AVIF), but the scale may not be  comparable. I saw someone say that he got larger files for WebP in Hugo vs AVIF. Reducing the quality to e.g. 60 when processing to AVIF could be the right medicine.

This proposal is to allow setting quality per format in `hugo.toml`, which would allow us to have different defaults.

Here's what Claude has to say:


>The scales aren't perceptually equivalent. libwebp Q75 is its conventional default and "good lossy" sweet spot. libavif/avifenc defaults to Q60, and Q60–70 in AV1 is widely considered comparable in perceived quality to WebP Q75 — and AVIF typically wins on size at that operating point. By picking Hugo's universal quality=75 default for AVIF, we land ~15 points above where libavif's own designers anchor "default good" — which produces visibly higher quality.

title: proposal: Preserve intentional empty maps in hugo config output
body:
PR #14934 drops empty sub-maps from `hugo config` output to reduce noise. However, this also removes `contentTypes`, whose entries are intentionally empty — they have no per-type options, so `ContentTypeConfig` is an empty struct by design.

Proposed fix: in `removeZeroVAlues`, distinguish between maps that are *originally* empty (intentional, preserve them) and maps that *became* empty after their zero-valued entries were stripped (noise, remove them). The #14934 behavior is otherwise unchanged.

With this fix, `hugo config` output includes the `contentTypes` section regardless of output format, restoring the behavior from v0.161.1. Users who discovered the `--printZero` workaround would no longer need it for this section.

For example, this command:

```sh
hugo config --format toml | grep -i contentTypes
```

Should produce this output:

```toml
[contenttypes]
  [contenttypes.'text/asciidoc']
  [contenttypes.'text/html']
  [contenttypes.'text/markdown']
  [contenttypes.'text/org']
  [contenttypes.'text/pandoc']
  [contenttypes.'text/rst']
```

Without this functionality it is difficult to determine which are enabled/disabled.

title: Trace view: display `service.namespace` alongside `service.name` in span labels
body:
**Why is this needed:**

In Kubernetes environments and other multi-tenant setups, it is common for the same `service.name` to exist across multiple namespaces. The [OpenTelemetry semantic conventions](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/resource/service/#service-namespace) define `service.namespace` (Stable as of semconv v1.40.0) as a standard resource attribute for disambiguating services that share a name:

> *"A string value having a meaning that helps to distinguish a group of services. `service.name` is expected to be unique within the same namespace."*

The OTel spec defines the `(service.namespace, service.name, service.instance.id)` triplet as globally unique, making `service.namespace` a first-class part of service identity. The [OTel Entity Data Model](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/entities/data-model/) also lists `service.namespace` as an identifying attribute for the `service.instance` entity type.

**Important note:** `service.namespace` is **not** equivalent to `k8s.namespace.name`. Per the OTel semantic conventions, `service.namespace` is an **organizational/logical grouping** — for example, a team name or business domain that owns a group of services. It is set explicitly by the application or deployment pipeline. `k8s.namespace.name` is the Kubernetes namespace where the workload runs, which is an infrastructure-level concept. While they *may* coincide in some environments, they are semantically distinct and should not be conflated.

Currently, the trace waterfall/timeline view in the traces panel only displays `service.name` in span labels, hover tooltips, and the expanded span detail. When multiple services share the same `service.name` but differ by `service.namespace`, they appear identical in the trace view, making it difficult to distinguish which service a span belongs to during troubleshooting.

**What would you like to be added:**

Display `service.namespace` alongside `service.name` in the trace waterfall when present in the span's resource attributes. Suggested format: `namespace/service-name` (consistent with Kubernetes conventions).

The implementation should coalesce across known attribute key variants. While the OTel semconv canonical attribute is `service.namespace`, some instrumentation pipelines (e.g. Prometheus-to-OTLP conversion) may emit `service.namespace.name` instead. The resolution logic should check both, preferring the canonical name:

```
namespace = process.tags['service.namespace'] ?? process.tags['service.namespace.name']
```

Specific locations that would benefit from this change:

1. **Span row label** in the waterfall timeline (`SpanBarRow`) — currently renders only `serviceName`
2. **Hover tooltip** (`labelDetail` in `SpanBarRow`) — currently renders `serviceName::operationName`
3. **Expanded span detail** overview (`SpanDetail`) — currently shows `Service: serviceName`
4. **Color assignment** (`VirtualizedTraceView`) — consider using `namespace/serviceName` as the color key so same-named services in different namespaces get distinct colors
5. **`showServiceName` logic** (`VirtualizedTraceView`) — should also trigger when namespace differs between consecutive spans

The display should be additive: if neither `service.namespace` nor `service.namespace.name` is present in the trace data, behavior remains unchanged (just `service.name`).

**Who is this feature for?**

Users running services across multiple Kubernetes namespaces or other multi-tenant environments where `service.name` alone is not unique. This is standard practice in OpenTelemetry-instrumented environments that follow the [service semantic conventions](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/resource/service/).

title: Share the green node cache
body:
I've been looking at ways to reduce RA memory use, because for my usecase it's regularly using >80GB! It has to dip into swap and performance tanks.

Right now, rust analyzer always uses `GreenNodeBuilder::default()`, which creates a new `NodeCache` for every file/text section.

I ran into issues implementing it the "right" way because I couldn't figure out how to get a `NodeCache` into the database methods (such as `base-db:lib.rs:parse`).

So, to run some quick benchmarks just to see if it's worth it, I implemented cache sharing the "wrong" way (using a global static mutex).
This gave a modest performance increase, and a substantial reduction in peak memory.

I also tried:
- interning green nodes when they are "mutated" with methods such as `splice_children`. This seems promising for continuous running. Cache hitrate for mutations was 45-60% depending on the repo, and didn't cause noticable perf degradation.
- Disabling or tweaking `>3 children` NodeCache heuristic. Disabling gave another big win in peak memory, but cost a lot of performance, tweaking is better.

Running rust-analyzer analysis-stats on itself in release mode:
Metric | Baseline | Global Cache | Global Cache Without Heuristic | Global Cache With Heuristic 4
-- | -- | -- | -- | --
Peak Memory | 4675.54MB | 4083.73MB (-12.7%) | 3739.20MB (-20.0%) | 3930.96MB (-16%)
Idle Memory (post LRU clear) | 2908MB | 2869MB (-1.3%) | 2863MB (-1.5%) | 2867MB (-1.4%)
NodeCache::node hitrate | 44.27% | 72.51% | 83.60% | 76.62%
NodeCache::token hitrate | 87.40% | 98.38% | 98.38% | 98.38%
Runtime | 87.37s | 82.05s (-6.1%) | 91.93s (+5.2%) | 81.60s (-6.6%)

Because duplication rate grows with codebase size, the memory reduction *should* grow superlinearly.
I chose a larger repo, but not so large to use swap, to avoid skewing the performance metrics.
Stats from a larger repo:
Metric | Baseline | Global Cache | Global Cache Without Heuristic | Global Cache With Heuristic 4
-- | -- | -- | -- | --
Peak Memory | 23015.48MB | 20466.32MB (-11.1%) | 17741.96MB (-22.9%) | 19970.84MB (-13.2%)
Idle Memory (post LRU clear) | 11944MB | 11936MB (-0.1%) | 11927MB (-0.1%) | 11933MB (-0.1%)
NodeCache::node hitrate | 44.30% | 71.13% | 87.33% | 76.23%
NodeCache::token hitrate | 89.38% | 99.31% | 99.31% | 99.31%
Runtime | 148.49s | 145.36s (-2.1%) | 167.40s (+12.7%) | 144.28s (-2.8%)

I didn't run any benchmarks for continuous editing, but they should benefit even more from this due to the fact they do small re-parses, so cache sharing has more benefit.

title: Be more lazy with the construction of inlay hint properties

title: Import suggestions within a function call should use function argument types to prioritize suggestions
body:
Say we've got some AtomicUsize, and we call `fetch_add` with `1` and `Ordering` (not yet imported), and then press Ctrl+Space at the `[HERE]` position

```rust
NEXT_STR_ID.fetch_add(1, Ordering[HERE])

Currently, it suggests `core::cmp::Ordering` as the top result, and then `core::sync::atomic::Ordering` after that. While the `core::cmp::Ordering` is perhaps used more commonly overall, or it just sorts earlier alphabetically, since the argument type of the second argument of `fetch_add` actually matches one of the suggestions already in the list (the atomic ordering type), that suggestion should get top priority.

title: Refactor our eager macro infra
body:
The current approach has some drawbacks, one being it is a complete mess :) Though I think a proper refactor needs to also look at our macro resolution loop in general unfortunately, or maybe the design of rust macro resolution loop is just incompatible with a nice IDE story. 

The way things work right now is that we effectively take input token trees of eager macros and reparse them as comma separated expressions and set that as the expansion of a fake input macro call for the actual eager macro call. We then expand all macros we find in that expansion ***manually*** and replacing the calls with the actual expansion and finally we write this expansion into a specific eager expansion field of a macro call loc whereas that macro call loc represents the actual macro invocation. This manual editing of the syntax  tree is a mess that we should not need to do, but it is currently somewhat necessary as we can't defer resolving the macro calls to the standard expansion query as that would end in cycles. (In the rust compiler eager macro expansions basically just tap back into the macro resolution loop transparently, we don't have this luxury)

This current approach also has the problem that we are unable to resolve the eagerly expanded macros in the IDE layer as they effectively do not exist in any records (fun fact, a similar problem will exist for the proc-macro equivalent [TokenStream::expand_epr](https://doc.rust-lang.org/proc_macro/struct.TokenStream.html#method.expand_expr), though there we can't really fix anything up from our side, https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/90765).

The current eager implementation lives here https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-analyzer/blob/master/crates/hir-expand/src/eager.rs

title: Custom magic completions
body:
the build in magic completions are amazing,
but when working with some libraries i end up wanting more magic completions specific to that library
(e.g. bevy, where a lot of simple plugins are 50% boilerplate and a lot of my `Component`s are newtypes with nearly identical derives),

custom magic completions would essentially add magic completion support for every single crates.io that needs them (as long as the user is willing to write some configuration files)

i'm not sure what the best way to implement this feature is, but the way i'd imagine it would be:
* a new file type (maybe `.rsmagic`, but that's for future bikeshedding) that contains the result of the completion,
 with a special character or set of characters that is not valid rust representing the points-you-jump-to-when-you-press-tab (what is their correct name?),
the first jump thing is where your cursor ends up after activating the completion
(this feature is already used in the std magic `tmod`, you immediately jump to the test functions name,
a more advanced magic may generate multiple things that the user needs to jump to and name)
* the trigger of the magic is just the file's name
(which makes finding the files for custom completions easier, just type their name into your file manager's search bar and it'll find wherever you put them)
* a new config option (e.g. `magic-completions`) that is a list of paths to magic completions to load.
* magic files are not `.toml` because they are not structured data,
and trying to put rust source code into a toml string sounds frustrating.

i'm currently busy with GMTK 2026 (which only lasts for a few days), but if it isn't too difficult i may try implementing this myself (which would be my first contribution to any rust project) once i'm done.

title: Stdlib macro expansion broken on nightly
body:
**Disclosure**: I used Claude to diagnose my issue but the report below is written by me, and Claude's findings make sense to me.

I use Zed as my editor which regularly downloads a recent, standalone, nightly version of r-a. Today it downloaded the 2026-07-20 nightly and I started getting type checking errors in places where stdlib macros are used in return position, e.g.

```rust
fn foo() -> String {
    format!("hello")
}
```

r-a would report as an error, saying it expected a `String` but got `()` instead. This is clearly wrong, and trying `cargo check`, `clippy` or actually compiling the code gave no errors or warnings.

I asked Claude to help find why r-a is showing macro invocations as `()` everywhere. At first it had some false starts, but then later it realized that the project in question is pinned to 1.92. It pointed me to https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-analyzer/pull/22784 as the PR that breaks resolution for stdlib macros for codebases pinned to <1.94, which makes sense to me.

The comment in that PR says "we only officially support that last stdlib, so I think it's fine to just not support older versions" which leads me to believe my setup (pinned toolchain, but running a recent r-a version) is an unsupported setup, however the current situation/resulting error message is very confusing. At least in zed these show up as "wrong type" errors. If this is an unsupported setup then r-a should warn about it at least.

Given

Current completion
