title: Docs: default image loader ignores image cache on new deployment, leading to higher usage costs
body:
### What is the documentation issue?

The documentation about Image Optimization with Vercel states that the [cache is not invalidated for remote images for a new deployment](https://vercel.com/docs/image-optimization#remote-images).
While this may be true and the image remains on the Vercel Edge Network, the default image loader in Next.js [appends the deployment id to the query url to the image optimization](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/44cb7dddfe386a6ddc307adf7c8b4ab3e9a00335/packages/next/src/shared/lib/image-loader.ts#L79-L83):
```ts
  return `${config.path}?url=${encodeURIComponent(src)}&w=${width}&q=${
    quality || 75
  }${
    process.env.NEXT_DEPLOYMENT_ID
      ? `&dpl=${process.env.NEXT_DEPLOYMENT_ID}`
      : ''
  }`
```
The result is that after every new deployment, a user's browser will see this as new image and will not use it's local cache.

This may be a documentation issue, where the actual implementation is not fully documented, or it may be a bug or feature request, to allow the author to opt out of using the deployment id in the default loader.

A workaround for this is to write a [custom loader](https://nextjs.org/docs/pages/api-reference/components/image#loader) that does the same as the Next.js default loader, with the exception of adding the deployment id.

### Is there any context that might help us understand?

Vercel bills projects for (amongst others) number of edge requests, number of image optimizations and transferred data. If every deployment will cause all visitors to download images again _even if they have not been changed_, this will create unnecessary charges.

### Does the docs page already exist? Please link to it.

https://vercel.com/docs/image-optimization#remote-images

> note that if you _reassign_ `counter` instead of updating it, you will 'break the link

> Svelte will warn you if you get it wrong.

```svelte
<script>
  import Child from './Child.svelte';
  import { setCounter } from './context.ts';

  let counter = $state({ count: 0 });

  // This reference only captures the initial value of `counter`. Did you mean to reference it inside a closure instead?
  // https://svelte.dev/e/state_referenced_locally
  setCounter(counter);
</script>

<button onclick={() => (counter = { count: (counter.count += 1) })}>
  increment
</button>

<Child />
```

I learned this the hard way by checking that `$state.raw` and `$derived` do not work with the context API.

### Describe the proposed solution

If possible, provide a better warning message.

title: docs: clarify `$derived` `await` examples, dependency tracking
body:
### Describe the problem

## 1

> An exception is that independent `$derived` expressions will update independently, even though they will run sequentially when they are first created:

```js
// these will run sequentially the first time,
// but will update independently
let a = $derived(await one());
let b = $derived(await two());
```

### 1-1

'run sequentially' is confusing.

For example, the promises can be created sequentially, but `b` can resolve first. The truth is:

> ...the second `$derived` will not be created until the first one has resolved.

Why not be specific like the quote in [`await_waterfall` docs](https://svelte.dev/docs/svelte/runtime-warnings#Client-warnings-await_waterfall)?

Clarification is needed because `$derived` isn't vanilla JavaScript.

```js
// this is intuitive. `two` is called after `one` is resolved.
await one();
await two();

// this is not intuitive
$derived(await one());
$derived(await two());
```

### 1-2

'update independently' is confusing.

Can `one` and `two` rerun? They don't have any dependencies.

```js
$derived(await one());
$derived(await two());
```

Example from query remote function seems better:

```js
let a = $derived(await one());
const post = $derived(await getPost(params.slug)); // params.slug is the dependency
```

## 2

> Anything read synchronously inside the `$derived` expression (or `$derived.by` function body) is considered a _dependency_ of the derived state.

Claude is complaining that `params.slug` is not read synchronously, thus not a dependency.

```js
$derived(await getPost(params.slug));
```

What are considered dependencies in async Svelte and `$derived`?

## Note

I believe I've used `await` inside `$derived.by` as an alternative to `untrack`. Maybe this should be warned on Svelte 5 to 6 migration? I didn't see it in the breaking changes section.

### Describe the proposed solution

See above

### Importance

title: Explain why `$bindable` shouldn't be often used
body:
https://svelte.dev/docs/svelte/$bindable tells:

> Ordinarily, props go one way, from parent to child. This makes it easy to understand how data flows around your app.
>
> In Svelte, component props can be bound, which means that data can also flow up from child to parent. This isn’t something you should do often, but it can simplify your code if used sparingly and carefully.

I think it misses an explanation why it could be done but shouldn't be done often. Or just don't tell anything ?

Actually I see it as a big topic, because I feel that bidirectional binding allows local source of truth and component responsibility, which is the state of art of OOP / SASS / API. I've yet to be convinced why suddenly with UI it's different and the flow should only go one way, because it equals to global variables, which is known to be the enemy of scalability and responsibility.

title: `to_json`: `timedelta_mode` and `temporal_mode` break documented behavior
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

`pydantic_core.to_json` (and `to_jsonable_python`) documents `timedelta_mode` and `temporal_mode` as independent parameters governing disjoint type sets:

> - `timedelta_mode`: How to serialize `timedelta` objects, either `'iso8601'` or `'float'`.
> - `temporal_mode`: How to serialize datetime-like objects (`datetime`, `date`, `time`), either `'iso8601'`, `'seconds'`, or `'milliseconds'`.

(This is what both the [API docs](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/api/pydantic-core/pydantic_core/) and the shipped `_pydantic_core.pyi` type stub say.)

Given that contract, `to_json(..., timedelta_mode="float", temporal_mode="iso8601")` should serialize `datetime`/`date`/`time` as ISO 8601 strings and `timedelta` as a float. Instead, `datetime`/`date`/`time` are **also** coerced to unix-timestamp floats, `timedelta_mode="float"` silently overrides `temporal_mode="iso8601"` for all temporal types.

There is no combination of the two parameters that yields ISO datetimes with float-second timedeltas, even though the documented parameters imply there should be.

**Root cause / regression.** This regressed in [#1743](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/pull/1743). Before that PR, `SerializationConfig` had a dedicated `timedelta_mode: TimedeltaMode` field and `to_json` had no `temporal_mode` parameter, so `timedelta_mode` was genuinely independent. #1743 replaced the dedicated field with a single unified `temporal_mode` and retrofitted `timedelta_mode` as a legacy alias that maps into it.

Either the docs/`.pyi` should be corrected to state that `timedelta_mode` is a deprecated alias that affects all temporal types, or (preferably) `timedelta` should retain an independent setting so the documented behavior holds. Personally I have a requirement to be able to set the `timedelta` format independent of the other `datetime` types.

### Example Code

```Python
import datetime
import pydantic_core

payload = {
    "dt": datetime.datetime(2026, 7, 9, 12, 0, 0),
    "d": datetime.date(2026, 7, 9),
    "t": datetime.time(12, 0, 0),
    "td": datetime.timedelta(hours=1, minutes=30),
}

# Per the docs: temporal_mode governs dt/d/t; timedelta_mode governs td.
actual = pydantic_core.to_json(
    payload, timedelta_mode="float", temporal_mode="iso8601"
).decode()

expected = '{"dt":"2026-07-09T12:00:00","d":"2026-07-09","t":"12:00:00","td":5400.0}'

print("actual  :", actual)
print("expected:", expected)
assert actual == expected, "timedelta_mode='float' wrongly coerced datetime/date/time to floats"
# AssertionError: actual == {"dt":1783598400.0,"d":1783555200.0,"t":43200.0,"td":5400.0}
```

import pydantic

### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

The documentation section ["Using the Field() function to describe function parameters"](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/validation_decorator/#using-the-field-function-to-describe-function-parameters) states that when `default_factory` is specified with `Field`, `Field` shouldn't be nested with in `Annotated`. However, as Pydantic at 2.9.2, I am able to do the following without any problem.

```python
from datetime import datetime

from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import Field, validate_call


@validate_call
def when(dt: Annotated[datetime, Field(default_factory=datetime.now)]):
    return dt

print(type(when()))
#> <class 'datetime.datetime'>
```

which is different than what is stated in the doc and the included example of 

```python
from datetime import datetime

from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import Field, ValidationError, validate_call


@validate_call
def how_many(num: Annotated[int, Field(gt=10)]):
    return num


try:
    how_many(1)
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e)
    """
    1 validation error for how_many
    0
      Input should be greater than 10 [type=greater_than, input_value=1, input_type=int]
    """


@validate_call
def when(dt: datetime = Field(default_factory=datetime.now)):
    return dt


print(type(when()))
#> <class 'datetime.datetime'>
```

### Example Code

_No response_

### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

```Text
▶ python -c "import pydantic.version; print(pydantic.version.version_info())"
             pydantic version: 2.9.2
        pydantic-core version: 2.23.4
          pydantic-core build: profile=release pgo=false
                 install path: /Users/isaac/Library/Application Support/hatch/env/virtual/dandisets-linkml-status-tools/lEMG0Emx/dandisets-linkml-status-tools/lib/python3.10/site-packages/pydantic
               python version: 3.10.15 (main, Nov 22 2024, 12:40:20) [Clang 16.0.0 (clang-1600.0.26.4)]
                     platform: macOS-15.1.1-arm64-arm-64bit
             related packages: typing_extensions-4.12.2
                       commit: unknown
```

So the documentation is either outdated or Pydantic is behaving unexpectedly in this aspect.

title: docs: timedelta spec string is incorrect
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

The documentation for the accepted timedelta formats seems wrong or outdated: https://docs.pydantic.dev/2.9/api/standard_library_types/#datetimetimedelta

While I assume the ISO format parsing works fine, I was interested in the alternate format listed:
`[-][DD]D[,][HH:MM:]SS[.ffffff]`

With the current docs giving the following examples:
- `1d,01:02:03.000004`
- `1D01:02:03.000004`
- `01:02:03`

Let's examine some definite discrepancies:
1. The example `01:02:03` doesn't satisfy the mandatory `D` in the spec string.
2. From that example and the spec (`[HH:MM:]SS`) I'd expect to be able use just `12` to mean 12 seconds. That doesn't work.

I suspect `[-][[DD]D,]HH:MM:SS[.ffffff]` more closely reflects what's currently accepted, although i haven't rigurously verified it.

Also, mixing the same letters for digit placeholders and literals here (e.g. `D`) makes for bad readability, but maybe there's a technical reason for it?

### Example Code

```Python
import pydantic

from datetime import timedelta


class Model(pydantic.BaseModel):
    td: timedelta


# docs:  [-][DD]D[,][HH:MM:]SS[.ffffff]


# let's run through the doc examples first.
for s in [
  '1d,01:02:03.000004',
  '1D01:02:03.000004',
  '01:02:03',
]:
    # all of these do work correctly.
    assert Model(td=s)


worked = {}
# i would expect at least one of these to work
for s in [
    "1",
    "01",
    "12",
    "12.123456",
    "012",
    "112",
    "D12",
    "0,12",
    "0d12",
    "0d,12",
    "1,12",
    "1d12",
    "1d,12",
    "12D12",
    "12312",
    "1,12s",
    "1d12s",
    "1d,12s",
]:
    try:
        worked[s] = Model(td=s)
    except Exception as ex:
        print(f"Failed to parse {s!r}:\n{ex}\n")

# but it doesn't
assert not worked
```

title: `model_json_schema` not including `computed_field`
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

The `model_json_schema` method does not include fields decorated with `@computed_field`.

According to the [Pydantic documentation](https://docs.pydantic.dev/2.9/concepts/fields/#the-computed_field-decorator):

_"The [computed_field](https://docs.pydantic.dev/2.9/api/fields/#pydantic.fields.computed_field) decorator can be used to include [property](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#property) or [cached_property](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functools.html#functools.cached_property) attributes when serializing a model or dataclass. The property will also be taken into account in the JSON Schema."_

However, when using `model_json_schema`, the computed field does not appear in the output. This behaviour is inconsistent with the documentation.

### Expected Behaviour:
The `computed_field` should be included in the output schema when using `model_json_schema`.

### Example Code

```Python
from pydantic import BaseModel, computed_field


class Box(BaseModel):
    width: float
    height: float
    depth: float

    @computed_field
    @property  
    def volume(self) -> float:
        return self.width * self.height * self.depth

Box.model_json_schema()
```

title: The docs should treat "FieldValidatorModes" more clearly, as they do for Model Validator Modes ("Literal['wrap', 'before', 'after']")
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [X] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

Hi, thanks for the incredible work on this library! 

### The Problem

I was recently implementing some Field Validators for the first time, and the docs are frustratingly vague when it comes to the modes -- the tutorial doesn't give any examples for modes other than the default, and reference doesn't even say what the options are ([before, after, wrap, plain](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/19f7d414c58d6af544f39c3e4a0e62b0dca6ab7f/pydantic/functional_validators.py#L392)), instead just giving the name of the convenience typedef "FieldValidatorModes". There's some great discussion for *model* validator modes, but A) it should be in both places or linked from one to the other, and B) there's no discussion whatsoever of the "plain" type, since it's only available for field validators. Which is extra confusing because the default is "after", not "plain"! 

### The Solution

Assuming I didn't miss the documentation (super possible), I think the change here should primarily be a documentation one (specifically to [`/api/functional_validators`](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/api/functional_validators/#pydantic.functional_validators.model_validator) and [`/concepts/validators`](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/validators/#field-validators)). 

One could argue that the direct, typedef-less approach from @adriangb's April 2023 [commit implementing ModelValidator](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/commit/7232fadc3e2f9f38497e47216e0da311f23339bb#diff-ca272dc261af03011fed42df0a75b39dec2bd2710419a7c7bcfb54cc69bca8b6R128) could/should be applied to FieldValidator too, but that's obviously only an internal concern. **At the very least, I would passionately request:**

1. Listing the four options in the docs somewhere instead of/in addition to the typedef name
2. An explanation of the "plain" mode
3. And a clarification that the function signature does not change for `field_validator(mode="before")` / `field_validator(mode="after")` like it does for `model_validator(mode="before")` / `model_validator(mode="after")`.**

I'd offer to help out myself / propose a pull request, but I don't have time to setup your dev system, so I'm leaving this instead. Will try to come back to it sometime if y'all are too busy :)

title: Unable to apply constraint 'strict' to schema of type 'union'
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Hi, I am trying to use a union type with `strict=False` in my schema and am not sure what the recommended workflow is.

I have the following model:
```py
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field, Strict, field_validator
from typing_extensions import Annotated


class MyBaseModel(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(strict=True)


class Model1(MyBaseModel):
    a: int | tuple[int, int] = Field(default=(1, 2))
```

Now it can happen that `a` is passed as a list instead of a tuple. I usually handle this with:

```py
class Model2(MyBaseModel):
    a: int | tuple[int, int] = Field(default=(1, 2), strict=False)
```

But this raises `RuntimeError: Unable to apply constraint 'strict' to schema of type 'union'`

Only annotating the tuple doesn't work either:
```py
class Model3(MyBaseModel):
    a: int | Annotated[tuple[int, int], Strict(False)] = Field(default=(1, 2))

Model3(a=[1, 2])
```
This raises:
```
pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 2 validation errors for Model3
a.int
  Input should be a valid integer [type=int_type, input_value=[1, 2], input_type=list]
    For further information visit https://errors.pydantic.dev/2.9/v/int_type
a.tuple[int, int]
  Input should be a valid tuple [type=tuple_type, input_value=[1, 2], input_type=list]
    For further information visit https://errors.pydantic.dev/2.9/v/tuple_type
```

---

So my current workaround is to add a `field_validator` but this is cumbersome:
```py
class Model4(MyBaseModel):
    a: int | tuple[int, int] = Field(default=(1, 2))

    @field_validator("a", mode="before")
    @classmethod
    def transform_a(cls, v) -> int | tuple[int, int]:
        if isinstance(v, list):
            return tuple(v)
        return v

Model4(a=[1, 2])
```

What is confusing to me is that setting `strict=False` in the base config works without error:
```py
class MyBaseModel(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(strict=False)


class Model1(MyBaseModel):
    a: int | tuple[int, int] = Field(default=(1, 2))

Model1(a=[1, 2])
```

title: model_validator mode="before" applied in the wrong order (from current class to base)
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

In pydantic v1, if we declared a root_validator with pre=True in Base model and in a subclass, it would first call the base root validator, and then the subclass one. It makes sense to e.g. customize some logic in all models

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, root_validator


class Base(BaseModel):
    x: int
    y: str

    @root_validator(pre=True)
    @classmethod
    def base_validator(cls, values):
        print("CALL 1")
        values["x"] = 1
        return values


class Model(Base):

    @root_validator(pre=True)
    @classmethod
    def model_validator(cls, values):
        print("CALL 2")
        values["x"] = 2
        return values


model = Model(x=3, y="a")

print(model)
```

Outputs first CALL 1, then CALL 2, as expected

But in pydantic v2, it's vice versa: first the subclass model_validator is called, and only then in BaseModel. It's counter-intuitive

Maybe there's a way to workaround this, but I was using it to workaround another issue: when using from_attributes=True, `model_validator` with `mode="before"` receives a model object instead of a dictionary, so my custom logic doesn't expect this and I need to make the same conversions pydantic-core does here: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/blob/bb67044c67b705d3ac7990ef067deb786e8d5afe/src/input/return_enums.rs#L293-L331

### Example Code

```Python
from pydantic import BaseModel, model_validator


class Base(BaseModel):
    x: int
    y: str

    @model_validator(mode="before")
    @classmethod
    def base_validator(cls, values):
        print("CALL 1")
        values["x"] = 1
        return values


class Model(Base):

    @model_validator(mode="before")
    @classmethod
    def model_validator(cls, values):
        print("CALL 2")

title: Clarification Needed: Differentiation Between Types and Constraints in Documentation
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Hey there!

I've been working with Pydantic and came across something a bit confusing in the documentation.
I noticed that some types listed in the [Pydantic Types documentation](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/api/types/#pydantic.types.StringConstraints) are actually data classes, like `StringConstraints`. While types like `PositiveInt` work as expected when used directly, trying to use `StringConstraints` as a type throws an error.

Here’s a small example:

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError, StringConstraints

class Model(BaseModel):
    name: StringConstraints(to_lower=True, strip_whitespace=True)

try:
    print(Model(name="Aa    "))
except ValidationError as ex:
    print(ex)
```

This gives me:

```
AttributeError: 'StringConstraints' object has no attribute '__mro__'
```

However, using `Annotated` works fine:

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, StringConstraints
from typing import Annotated
 
class Model(BaseModel):
    name: Annotated[str, StringConstraints(to_lower=True, strip_whitespace=True)]
```

So, my understanding is that `StringConstraints` is not actually a type but more like metadata or constraints. But listing it alongside actual types like `PositiveInt` in the documentation is a bit misleading.

It would be super helpful if the docs could clarify this a bit more—maybe add a hint that data classes like `StringConstraints` need to be used with `Annotated` and aren’t meant to be used as direct types.

Thanks a lot!

body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Hi everybody,
first off, thank you for your amazing work on `pydantic` and on the other products!

I would like to point out a possible (I apologize if this is not the case and I'm missing something) inconsistency in the documentation at https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/fields/#field-aliases, where the note specifies that 

> !!! note "Alias precedence and priority"
      In case you use `alias` together with `validation_alias` or `serialization_alias` at the same time,
      the `validation_alias` will have priority over `alias` for validation, and `serialization_alias` will have priority
      over `alias` for serialization.

> **You may also set `alias_priority` on a field to change this behavior.**

As far as I could experiment, there's no way you can leverage on `alias_priority` if you don't use an `AliasGenerator`. If that's effectively the case, IMO the final statement in the note might be somewhat misleading because the section does not deal with alias generators, whose _alias precedence_ behaviours are indeed well described at https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/alias/#alias-precedence.

As a possible corroboration to that, tests at `pydantic/tests/test_aliases.py` do not reference `alias_priority` when an `AliasGenerator` is not involved (if not for testing that `alias_priority=2` by default when `repr`esenting a model).

### Example Code

```Python
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class Model(BaseModel):
    first_name: str = Field(
        alias="firstName",
        validation_alias="FIRST_NAME",
        serialization_alias="f_name",
        alias_priority=1
    )


model = Model(firstName="Pippo")   # ValidationError, no way to tweak alias_priority to be able to validate via plain_alias
print(model.model_dump())
print(model.model_dump(by_alias=True))   # Serialization via serialization_alias only

title: Model validator is ignored during inheritance
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

When I have a parent and child class that both implement `model_validator`, the parent's model validator is ignored in the child class. 

This can be a source of bugs as one might expect the parent's validation to run together with the child's validation.

### Example Code

```Python
from pydantic import BaseModel, model_validator

class Sub(BaseModel):
    positive: int

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    @classmethod
    def model_validator(cls, v):
        if v.positive <= 0:
            raise ValueError()
        return v

class Main(Sub):
    negative: int

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    @classmethod
    def model_validator(cls, v):
        if v.negative >= 0:
            raise ValueError()
        return v

# throws an error
sub = Sub(positive=-1)

# doesn't throw an error
main = Main(positive=-1, negative=-2)
```

title: ValidationError Input should be None when field is named as type inside Optional
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

I've encountered a strange `ValidationError` while using a model with a `bytes` field and an `Optional[bytes]` annotation.

Please consider the examples below. 

It seems the issue is not with using a built-in type as a field name (which is doubtful but okay), but rather with the fact that the field name and the type inside `Optional` are the same.

I've also seen closed https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/7871, but the problem presents in the latest version of `pydantic`.

### Example Code

```Python
from typing import Optional

from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError

# OK
class M1(BaseModel):
    payload: Optional[str] = None


m1 = M1(payload='123')

# OK
class M2(BaseModel):
    payload: Optional[bytes] = None


m2 = M2(payload=b'123')

# Bug
class M3(BaseModel):
    str: Optional[str] = None


try:
    m3 = M3(str='123')
except ValidationError:
    # pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 1 validation error for MyModel
    # str
    #   Input should be None [type=none_required, input_value='123', input_type=str]
    #     For further information visit https://errors.pydantic.dev/2.7/v/none_required
    ...

# Bug
class M4(BaseModel):
    bytes: Optional[bytes] = None


try:
    m4 = M4(bytes=b'123')
except ValidationError:
    # pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 1 validation error for M4
    # bytes
    #   Input should be None [type=none_required, input_value=b'123', input_type=bytes]
    #     For further information visit https://errors.pydantic.dev/2.7/v/none_required
    ...

# OK
class M5(BaseModel):
    bytes: Optional[str] = None


m5 = M5(bytes='123')


class M(BaseModel):
    ...

# Bug
class M6(BaseModel):
    M: Optional[M] = None

try:
    m6 = M6(M=M())
except ValidationError:
    # pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 1 validation error for M6
    # M
    #  Input should be None [type=none_required, input_value=M(), input_type=M]
    #    For further information visit https://errors.pydantic.dev/2.7/v/none_required
    ...
```

body:
### First check * [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue. * [x] I used the GitHub search to find a similar issue and didn't find it. * [x] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search. * [x] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information. * [x] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer. * [x] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic](https://github.com/samuelcolvin/pydantic). * [x] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui). * [x] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc). * [x] After submitting this, I commit to: * Read open issues with questions until I find 2 issues where I can help someone and add a comment to help there. * Or, I already hit the "watch" button in this repository to receive notifications and I commit to help at least 2 people that ask questions in the future. * Implement a Pull Request for a confirmed bug. ### Description The Markdown docs have a lot of inline code sections dynamically included. Many of them use `hl_lines` to highlight lines, for example, to highlight from lines 5 to 10, and lines from 23 to 25: 
```Python hl_lines="5 6 7 8 9 10 23 24 25"
{!../../../docs_src/how_to_do_x/tutorial003.py!}
```
In a recent PR, @rkbeatss made me realize that `hl_lines` now supports ranges of highlighted lines. So, the example above could be: 
```Python hl_lines="5-10 23-25"
{!../../../docs_src/how_to_do_x/tutorial003.py!}
```
which is a lot easier to understand and maintain. ### The solution you would like I would like to replace all those `hl_lines` in the docs that highlight a range of lines with the new range syntax to make them easier to maintain and understand. ### Describe alternatives you've considered Leaving it as is, but all the updates for those docs are quite difficult as it's not obvious which numbers belong to a range and which are individual lines. Even more, when a line on the top is added (or removed), all those ranges change, increasing or decreasing. The new syntax would be a lot easier to update. With the current syntax (before the update) it's very easy to miss or break some of those line highlights.

title: Remove *, where it's not needed
body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem

Coming from this issue: https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/issues/817

The docs have some sections with functions using `*,` in the parameters.

It is explained here: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/path-params-numeric-validations/#order-the-parameters-as-you-need-tricks

But in other sections like: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/response-model/ the `*,` is not really needed and would probably just cause some confusion.

Remove the `*,` from function parameters in the docs at the places where it's not needed, i.e. the places where a function parameter with a default (e.g. a `Query()` or `Depends()`) does NOT come before a function parameter without a default value.

title: Set up translations for docs

Several community members have proposed and offered help adding translations to other languages.

Portuguese: #921 
Chinese: discussed with https://twitter.com/linupy1 on Twitter
Spanish: at least I would do it, I hope others would be willing to help :smile: 

### The solution you would like

I have to set up a simple way to add translations.

I think it will be adding a copy of the same MkDocs files for each language and including all that on a sub path.

It will probably include copying each original English file that is not translated and adding a note about its translation.

And there should also be a way to add a note about translations that need to be re-synchronized with the original English version.

There should also probably be a note about translations being provided by the community and that the "official" version is always English.

It would probably depend a lot on each PR getting several PR approvals by community members. I can verify and check Spanish and, to some extent, Portuguese. Not adding translations at all.

Waiting for MkDocs to have official support for translations https://github.com/mkdocs/mkdocs/issues/617 , but as this is a complex topic, I expect that to take some time. And we can have a simple version that works, at least just for FastAPI.

title: Add chat integration to the docs website
body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem

Is your feature request related to a problem? Nope.

Tom Christie shared the idea of having the Gitter chat integrated into the docs website, he implemented it for Starlette.

We should have something similar.

Here's his PR: https://github.com/encode/starlette/pull/834

### The solution you would like

Copy Tom's code :man_shrugging:  and integrate FastAPI's Gitter chat into the docs website.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

Not doing it. Here's my small rant:

So, a chat system has some problems, it's a bit chaotic, all the conversations are mixed in the same sequence/thread, some get lost and never answered, can't be searched easily as GitHub issues or StackOverflow questions, so many questions are asked again and again.

I can't make sure personally that all the questions are answered in the chat (even if after a long time), that I can with GitHub issues, even if it takes me a year.

And as it's very easy to ask a question there, many people ask in the chat even before searching in Google or the docs. And many times the questions are not very "well-formed" (e.g. not having a clear example of what the person is trying to achieve) and it takes several turns back and forth just to clarify the question itself. And all that that consumes time and effort from the people that are there to help, that could have been avoided or invested in helping someone with a more difficult question that doesn't have an answer with a Google search.

But...

There's a lot of people in the chat, they end up there, and there are several awesome community members helping each other there, constantly.

It seems that despite all the problems with a chat system, it somehow helps foster an active community. For example, it seems it's easier for a community member to answer a question in the chat than to go to StackOverflow and answer `fastapi` questions there, even when StackOverflow gives points and stuff. 

So, if the chat is helping, we should embrace it and put it in the docs. :man_shrugging:

https://gitter.im/tiangolo/fastapi?at=5e4d1705c2c73b70a44530ca

title: DOC: Incorrect missing-value representation in Python StringDtype documentation
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on `main` [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/)


### Location of the documentation

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/doc/source/user_guide/text.rst

### Documentation problem

The "Python storage with pd.NA values" section says that NA values are represented and behave as np.nan.
However, the example explicitly constructs StringDtype with na_value=pd.NA, and the following paragraph says the missing values are stored as pd.NA.
The implementation and tests also indicate that the Python-backed pd.NA variant stores and uses pd.NA semantics.

### Suggested fix for documentation

Replace:

> NA values in this array are represented and behave as `np.nan`.

with:

> NA values in this array are represented and behave as `pd.NA`.

This matches the `na_value=pd.NA` configuration used in the example and the following explanation that missing inputs are stored as `pd.NA`.

title: docs: Drop = from Nginx 404 configuration
body:
In the _Automatic Loading_ section of _Custom 404 page_ documentation, the configuration for Nginx is given as `error_page 404 = /404.html;`

This is correct, but sets the status code Nginx returns to the client to what requesting /404.html returns. I.e. if /404.html exists the status code is 200 OK.

When the configuration is changed to `error_page 404 /404.html;` (without the = ) Nginx returns the status code that matched the error_page configuration, which in this case is 404.

Detailed info about error_page configuration available in [Nginx documentation](http://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_core_module.html#error_page)

title: Docs: `merge` transformation page should clarify it does not join by labels; document the labelsToFields → merge → groupBy recipe
body:
### Page

https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/panels-visualizations/query-transform-data/transform-data/#merge-series-into-table

### Grafana version

12.4.2 (v2beta1 dashboard schema)

### What's confusing

The `merge` transformation reads as if it joins multi-query frames by shared labels, but it actually concatenates them as separate row blocks. For the common case of "I have multiple Prometheus instant queries that share label sets (e.g. account/region) and I want one row per shared-label tuple with each query's `Value` as its own column," `merge` alone produces a table where the same label tuples appear duplicated across rows — one block per query.

The canonical recipe to actually join is:

```
labelsToFields (mode: columns) → merge → groupBy (lastNotNull on each value column, grouping by the shared label columns)
```

This isn't shown anywhere obvious in the docs. New users (myself included) reach for `merge` first and end up confused by the output.

### Suggested doc improvement

On the `merge` page (and ideally on a more general "join queries by labels" page), add a short "merging vs joining" note showing:

- What `merge` does on its own (concatenates rows; does not dedupe by label).
- The `labelsToFields(columns) → merge → groupBy(lastNotNull)` pattern as the canonical recipe for joining multi-query Prometheus instant data by shared labels.
- A small worked example (e.g. two `up`-style queries with `instance`/`job` labels → one row per `(instance, job)` with both values as columns).

### Note

Filing as an end-user, not a maintainer. Happy to review a doc PR if useful.

title: Docs(SqlExpressions): Clarify limitations with frontend-only datasources
body:
## Overview

In [the SQL Expressions docs](https://github.com/grafana/grafana/blob/b5c500dca2fda3058ca012a46a20619c3c0d1f92/docs/sources/visualizations/panels-visualizations/query-transform-data/sql-expressions/index.md?plain=1#L62), we say:

> To work with SQL expressions, you must use data from a backend data source. In Grafana, a backend data source refers to a data source plugin or integration that communicates with a database, service, or API through the Grafana server, rather than directly from the browser (frontend).

This is correct, but there's an opportunity to give the user practical guidance, as it's not clear to users when they are working with a data source that's frontend-only.

## Suggested enhancement

I believe the most common frontend-only data source is the [`-- Dashboard --`](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/datasources/#dashboard) data source. Perhaps we could point out that queries using the Dashboard data source are not supported with SQL Expressions. In practical terms, providing this example should help users avoid the most likely source of friction with SQL Expressions + frontend data sources.

title: Document reference search for constructiors/initializations
Manual needs to be more helpful, friendly, and better organized
body:
rust-analyzer manual is pretty long: https://rust-analyzer.github.io/manual.html

It's useful as a reference, but is quite intimidating if you want to learn the tool. We should improve this, both in terms of logical organization, and in terms of HTML&CSS rendering. I am not experienced with it, so help would be much appreciated. 

I think ideally the manual shows a short pit of success, while giving the links to in-depth reference material. Here's a structure I have in mind:

First is quick start, which suggests choosing an editor (VS Code, Vim, Emacs). For a specific editor, we have a single blessed setup. After the setup, we have a short section show-casing the most important features (worksapce symbol, go to definiton, extend selection, running tests, triggering assists). This should be duplicated for editor, and serves two purposes -- teaches about the features and allows the new user to verify if the stuff is working. Aftre quick start and show case, we show how to configure rust-analyzer in the specific editor. After that, we show alterntive setups


After per-editor quick start, we probably want to re-create show case, with the emprasis on how it looks and why it is useful, rather than on which shourtcur do you use to trigger this. 

After universal show-case, we should have an index of features, which leads to specific pages for diagnostics, assists, etc.

After that, we should have troubleshooting and other stuff. 

As I've said, I am not an expert at this: if you think you see a better way to do this, feel free to suggest. The source for manual lives here: https://github.com/rust-analyzer/rust-analyzer/tree/master/docs/user.

It is render to a web document here: https://github.com/rust-analyzer/rust-analyzer.github.io

The code to move the manual from the first place to the second place is here: https://github.com/rust-analyzer/rust-analyzer/blob/91bfa4b154a9776a57f25071f03e68d4f9f5ef35/xtask/src/release.rs#L25-L50

title: LengthDelimitedCodec Builder doc examples (new/new_codec/new_read/new_write) still use broken length_adjustment(0)+num_skip(0) combo, corrupts frames
body:
LengthDelimitedCodec Builder doc examples (new/new_codec/new_read/new_write) still use broken length_adjustment(0)+num_skip(0) combo, corrupts frames

### Version
tokio-util 0.7.19, rustc 1.97.1, tokio-rs/tokio commit dd344a550c2c6ddc500a2a8ad2eca8e097795252

### Description

Four `Builder` method doc examples in `tokio-util/src/codec/length_delimited.rs` show `.length_adjustment(0)` combined with `.num_skip(0)` as a working configuration:

- `Builder::new` — lines 677-690
- `Builder::new_codec` — lines 951-961
- `Builder::new_read` — lines 977-990
- `Builder::new_write` — lines 1002-1017

    LengthDelimitedCodec::builder()
        .length_field_offset(0)
        .length_field_type::<u16>()
        .length_adjustment(0)   // default value
        .num_skip(0)
        .new_read(io);

This combination silently corrupts decoded frames: `num_skip(0)` means the length-header bytes are never advanced past, but `length_adjustment(0)` does not compensate by adding the header width back into the byte count that gets sliced off. The result is a decoded frame that includes the raw header bytes at the front and is short at the back, with the missing tail bytes leaking into the next frame's header.

### Reproduction

    let mut codec = LengthDelimitedCodec::builder()
        .length_field_offset(0)
        .length_field_type::<u16>()
        .length_adjustment(0)
        .num_skip(0)
        .new_codec();

    let mut buf = BytesMut::new();
    codec.encode(Bytes::from_static(b"hello world"), &mut buf).unwrap();
    let frame = codec.decode(&mut buf).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(frame, Some(BytesMut::from(&b"hello world"[..]))); // fails

Actual decoded output: `b"\0\x0bhello wor"` (header bytes prepended, "ld" truncated and left in the buffer to corrupt the next frame). Expected: `b"hello world"`.

This isn't caught by the doctests because they are compile-only (no assert/round-trip executed) — confirmed via `cargo test --doc --all-features`.

### Why this matters

These are the canonical examples a developer copies when first configuring `LengthDelimitedCodec::Builder`. Copying `new_codec`/`new_read`/`new_write` as shown produces a codec that silently corrupts every frame after the first.

### Prior history

This exact corruption mechanism was reported in #6604 and closed by #6638 (merged 2024-06-14). However, #6638 only fixed the module-level "Example 1–6" walkthroughs earlier in the file — it never touched these four `Builder::*` method-doc examples, which still contain the identical broken snippet on current master.

### Suggested fix

Apply the same fix #6638 used elsewhere in this file: either drop `.num_skip(0)` (falls back to the default skip-header behavior, matching Example 1), or add `.length_adjustment(2)` to account for the 2-byte u16 header width — and make the doctest actually execute and assert a round-trip, as #6638 did for the module-level examples.

Suggested labels: T-docs, A-tokio-util

title: `block_in_place` + `block_on` + `tokio::sync::Mutex` may lead to a deadlock
Release steps say to remove path deps
body:
We used to remove path dependencies in the `Cargo.toml` when releasing a crate. This was to ensure that the released crate does not depend on unreleased changes in other crates, as removing the path dependency makes CI compile it using the crates.io version of the dependency.

However, we've stopped doing this, and the big reason is that it doesn't work anymore. CI triggers errors such as this one when you try it:
```
error: There are multiple `tokio` packages in your project, and the specification `tokio` is ambiguous.
Please re-run this command with `-p <spec>` where `<spec>` is one of the following:
  file:///home/runner/work/tokio/tokio/tokio#1.49.0
  https://github.com/rust-lang/crates.io-index#tokio@1.49.0
Error: Process completed with exit code 101.
```
We should either fix CI so that we can continue doing it, or we should remove this instruction from the docs.

title: `TcpListener::bind` example in `TcpSocket` docs is no longer correct
body:
**Version**
1.48.0

**Platform**
N/A

**Description**
The [docs for `TcpSocket` say](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/blob/d709df25717e292609d93d4002a98232e63eccd3/tokio/src/net/tcp/socket.rs#L49):

> Calling `TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:8080")` is equivalent to:
>
> ```rust
> use tokio::net::TcpSocket;
>
> use std::io;
>
> #[tokio::main]
> async fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
>     let addr = "127.0.0.1:8080".parse().unwrap();
>
>     let socket = TcpSocket::new_v4()?;
>     // On platforms with Berkeley-derived sockets, this allows to quickly
>     // rebind a socket, without needing to wait for the OS to clean up the
>     // previous one.
>     //
>     // On Windows, this allows rebinding sockets which are actively in use,
>     // which allows "socket hijacking", so we explicitly don't set it here.
>     // https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/winsock/using-so-reuseaddr-and-so-exclusiveaddruse
>     socket.set_reuseaddr(true)?;
>     socket.bind(addr)?;
>
>     let listener = socket.listen(1024)?;
>
>     Ok(())
> }
> ```

But the backlog parameter was changed in mio in https://github.com/tokio-rs/mio/pull/1896. So 1024 is no longer used by `TcpListener::bind`.

I'm not sure how you'd like to fix this, since copying the logic from mio probably wouldn't be useful. Maybe a comment should be added here saying that the backlog size is actually platform-dependent?

title: Clarify the behavior of several `spawn_local` methods
body:
This issue is tracked by #7558, and it MUST be done before stabilizing the [`LocalRuntime`].

## What are the `spawn_local` methods?

[`tokio::task::spawn_local`] is used for spawn a `!Send` [`Future`] on the [`LocalSet`] or [`LocalRuntime`], and there are several methods call [`tokio::task::spawn_local`] internally.

* [`JoinSet::spawn_local`]
* [`JoinSet::spawn_local_on`]
* [`JoinMap::spawn_local`]
* [`JoinMap::spawn_local_on`]
* [`TaskTracker::spawn_local`]
* [`TaskTracker::spawn_local_on`]

## What should we do?

We need to update the docs to clarify the behavior when the methods above are called on the [`LocalRuntime`].

## What is the behavior on the [`LocalRuntime`]?

Invoking these methods on the [`LocalRuntime`] doesn't panic.

## What else do we need to do?

It would be better specifically reminding the authors of library crates to use these methods with caution, as calling them in their libraries may lead to their downstream panics, especially if their downstream uses a multi-threaded runtime.

title: Guideline for choosing between Current Thread Runtime and Local Runtime
body:
This issue is tracked by #7558, and it MUST be done before stabilizing the [`LocalRuntime`].

## What should we do?

We need to write a guide to advise downstream on when to choose [Current Thread Runtime] and when to choose [`LocalRuntime`].

## What is the difference between the [Current Thread Runtime] and [`LocalRuntime`]?

They both share the exact same scheduler implementation, which means that the [`LocalRuntime`] uses the scheduler of the [Current Thread Runtime].
The only difference is that the [`LocalRuntime`] is NOT [`Send`], while the [Current Thread Runtime] is.

## When to choose the [Current Thread Runtime]?

See <https://tokio.rs/tokio/topics/bridging> for the use case. In summary, downstream should choose the [Current Thread Runtime] when

* They need to call asynchronous code from synchronous code.
* AND they want to store the asynchronous runtime somewhere, to avoid creating a new runtime for each async call.
* AND the struct that holds the runtime needs to be [`Send`].

## When to choose the [`LocalRuntime`]?

For the majority of use cases other than those mentioned above, downstream should choose the [`LocalRuntime`] unless they are facing some issue.

[`LocalRuntime`]: https://docs.rs/tokio/1.47.1/tokio/runtime/struct.LocalRuntime.html
[Current Thread Runtime]: https://docs.rs/tokio/1.47.1/tokio/runtime/struct.Builder.html#method.new_current_thread
[`Send`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/1.89.0/core/marker/trait.Send.html

body:
mio's [documentation](https://docs.rs/mio/latest/mio/net/struct.TcpListener.html#method.bind) for `TcpListener::bind` clearly states that the TCP listener will set `SO_REUSEADDR` on Unix only, as this socket option has a different meaning on Windows.

Tokio's [documentation](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/blob/86528741f960b2425fe7168080744ff3f16cf195/tokio/src/net/tcp/listener.rs#L78) omits the fact that this is Unix-only, which can be confusing for users of the API who haven't consulted the mio documentation.

title: AsyncWrite documentation is confusing
body:
I was recently trying to understand `AsyncWrite` (specifically https://docs.rs/tokio/1.44.2/tokio/io/trait.AsyncWrite.html), and found the overview documentation unhelpful in places.

For example:

> The trait inherits from std::io::Write
It doesn't. (Technically, trait inheritance doesn't even exist.) I think this is trying to say that `AsyncWrite` is an async analog of the core of the `Write` trait.

> All non-blocking I/O objects must return an error when bytes cannot be written instead of blocking the current thread.
As the text below explains, they return `Pending`, not an error. 

And the term `nonblocking` isn't really defined, other than this sentence. I wonder if it would be better just to stick to `asynchronous`.

> This trait importantly means that the write method only works in the context of a future’s task.
This trait doesn't have a `write` method.

> Note that this trait also represents that the Write::flush method works very similarly to the write method
You can't call `std::Write::flush` (or `std::Write::write`) on an `AsyncWrite` object. This is presumably trying to say something about `poll_flush`.

> Utilities for working with AsyncWrite values are provided by AsyncWriteExt
They're not so much utilities as the methods that a user (rather than an implementor) of the trait would use.

(The documentation for `AsyncWriteExt` says "Callers will tend to import this trait instead of AsyncWrite", which might usefully be mentioned in the documentation for `AsyncWrite`.)

More importantly, this is where to look for versions of the `std::Write` methods that aren't directly represented in `AsyncWrite` - or at least some of them.


Would you be interested in a contribution that attempted to address these?

title: #[serde(tag=...)] attribute not rejected on structs
Document combination of custom (de)serializer for type in different crate
The serde crate's derive feature interacts poorly with 2018-style macro imports
body:
Say I have a crate that derives Serialize for one type, and has to manually implement it for another. I believe the "standard" way of doing this would be

```rust
use serde_derive::Serialize;
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct Foo(u32);

struct Bar(u32);

impl Serialize for Bar {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, s: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        self.0.to_string().serialize(s)
    }
}
```

This works fine in isolation, but if this crate is used alongside some other crate that activates serde's `derive` feature, it will stop compiling:

```
error[E0252]: the name `Serialize` is defined multiple times                                                                                                            
 --> src/lib.rs:2:13                                                                                                                                                    
  |                                                                                                                                                                     
1 | use serde_derive::Serialize;                                                                                                                                        
  |     ----------------------- previous import of the macro `Serialize` here                                                                                           
2 | use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};                                                                                                                                 
  |             ^^^^^^^^^ `Serialize` reimported here                                                                                                                   
  |                                                                                                                                                                     
  = note: `Serialize` must be defined only once in the macro namespace of this module                                                                                   
help: you can use `as` to change the binding name of the import                                                                                                         
  |                                                                                                                                                                     
2 | use serde::{Serialize as OtherSerialize, Serializer};                                                                                                               
  |             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^                                                                                                                             
                                                                                                                                                                        
error: aborting due to previous error                                                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                        
For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0252`. 
```

The crate can be made to compile in both scenarios by importing Serialize and Serializer from `serde::ser` rather than `serde`, but it seems like an easy thing to forget, and you're not going to notice until it breaks someone downstream that's trying to use your crate.

What do you think the right way of avoiding this is? Should the recommended approach change from depending on serde_derive to using the derive feature directly?

title: desktop: how to properly type a binding?
No way to opt out of global Node.js types (since 2.8.0)
body:
## Summary

Since v2.8.0, Deno includes the Node.js type lib globally by default, and there doesn't seem to be a way to opt out.

## Reproduction

```ts
const _timeout: number = setTimeout(() => {});
```

On Deno 2.8.0 or higher (currently 2.9.1), this fails with:

```
Type 'Timeout' is not assignable to type 'number'.
```

On 2.7.14 and earlier, it type-checks fine. `setTimeout` returning `number` matches the browser behavior.

## Background

I originally started writing this as a bug report. I assumed some package was importing the Node.js types and Deno was failing to exclude them. While isolating the issue, I realized the change was intentional:

> feat: include node lib by default and use NodeJS.Timeout for timers (#33823)

The node lib is pulled in via a `/// <reference lib="node" />` directive inside `lib.deno.shared_globals.d.ts`, so every Deno lib includes it. Setting `compilerOptions.lib` doesn't help, since you can't get Deno's globals without the Node.js types coming along.

I just realized this today after upgrading the Deno version of an old project, seeing Node.js type errors inside Deno truly feels like a bug. I was surprised how such an obvious bug could live until 2.9.1.

Turns out it was intentional. I have no idea why while there is `@types/node`.

## Why this matters

One of Deno's core promises (selling point) has always been browser API compatibility: web-standard APIs behaving the way they do in the browser. In the browser, `setTimeout` returns a `number`, and code written against web standards expects that. With this change, web-compatible code now type-errors under Deno, while Node-specific patterns are the ones that type-check.

Node.js compat is valuable, and I understand wanting `NodeJS.Timeout` patterns to work for people porting legacy code. But making the Node.js types global for everyone inverts the default: projects that don't touch `node:` at all (some on purpose) still get Node's type environment. Those who need it could opt in (as they already can with `@types/node`), rather than everyone else having no way to opt out.

## Expected

Either make the node lib opt-in, or at minimum provide a way to exclude it while keeping the Deno globals, so web-standard code can keep type-checking as it does in the browser.

If there will be a Node.js compat layer, that should be hidden from the user and should only apply to external packages until its not needed anymore.

title: Why does `deno run` use the network without the `--allow-net` flag (or including the --deny-net flag)
body:
I'm in the process of switching away from Node as much as possible, and came across a change to not use npx in favour of Deno.

```
deno run npm:wrangler pages blah blah
```

Per the docs: https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/node/

```
# deno run allows remote execution of a package from various locations,
# and can scoped to npm via the `npm:` specifier.
$ deno run -A npm:create-next-app@latest
```

This is the error after blocking the network connection:

```
error: Failed loading https://registry.npmjs.org/wrangler for package "wrangler"

Caused by:
    error sending request for url (https://registry.npmjs.org/wrangler): client error (Connect): tcp connect error: Bad file descriptor (os error 9)
```

npmjs isn't on the list of allowed URLS: https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security/#network-access


Now, I think the nuance here is that the docs specifically state "executing code"?
```
executing code can not make network requests, open network listeners or perform DNS resolution. This includes making HTTP requests, opening TCP/UDP sockets, and listening for incoming connections on TCP or UDP.
```

So, I'm guessing that the intention is that Deno itself can have all permissions, but just the thing that Deno is running can't? I have to admit, I was a bit surprised to see my network blocker pop up when running that command.

title: Creating a 100% self-contained binary
body:
Hi there,

I've been trying to create a 100% self-contained binary of my application for a while now with no success. My goal is to produce a binary file that is able to run in a server with no internet, but I've been facing a few issues here and there.

I've used the following command to produce a binary, and while this works, the binary produced is not 100% self contained:

```sh
> deno compile --allow-all --output compiled/service applications/service/run.ts
```

The output of this command is:

```sh
Compile file:///.../applications/service/run.ts to compiled/service/app

Embedded Files

app
├─┬ .deno_compile_node_modules (39.02MB - 35.77MB unique)
│ └─┬ localhost (39.02MB - 35.77MB unique)
… a huge file tree

Files: 54.22MB
Metadata: 13.08KB
Remote modules: 14.64MB
```

As it can be seen, there are about 15MB of remote modules, that will be retrieved when the application is executed for the first time. This is what I want to avoid.

**A few flags I’ve tried:**

- Add the `--vendor` flag to the `deno compile` command. Same result.
- Cache all dependencies and then run the `demo compile` command with the `--cached-only` flag. Same result.

**Weird and ugly workaround that partially works:**

I added the `”vendor”: true` option in the `deno.json` file. When I do this I see a `vendor` and a `node_modules` directories created. Then I created a custom `imports-vendor.json` file and then used the `--import-map imports-vendor.json` flag in the `deno compile` command. After all this I was able to get a binary file with less Remote modules. See the following output:

```sh
Compile file:///.../applications/service/run.ts to compiled/service/app

Embedded Files

app
├─┬ .deno_compile_node_modules (39.02MB - 35.77MB unique)
│ └─┬ localhost (39.02MB - 35.77MB unique)
… a huge file tree

Files: 68.2MB
Metadata: 13.39KB
Remote modules: 1000.78KB
```

This workaround isn’t working very well, as for some reason some of the vendor libraries were randomly (?????) renamed (e.g. #class_5c123.ts, instead of the original `Class.ts`) breaking all the imports and making the `deno compile` command fail. I had to rename a bunch of files to get this thing working. Again, not a very pleasant way to produce a stand-alone binary.

**My questions are then:**

- Is there a way I can create a binary file that never retrieves remote modules?
- How can I embed every single dependency in this binary file?


Info about my setup:

```sh
deno 2.2.14 (long term support, release, aarch64-apple-darwin)
v8 13.5.212.10-rusty
typescript 5.7.3

title: deno compile ignores -o <name> when compilation is run from outside the project root (input file is not in the cwd)
body:
Version: Deno 2.3.6

### Reproduction Steps

1. Create a directory and initialize a Deno project:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/work/foo
cd ~/work/foo
deno init
cd ..
```

2. From outside the project root (`~/work`), run:

```bash
deno compile foo/main.ts -o out.bin
```

---

### Observed Behavior

```bash
~/work ❯ deno compile foo/main.ts -o out.bin
Check file:///home/user/work/foo/main.ts
Compile file:///home/user/work/foo/main.ts to foo
error: Could not compile to file 'foo' because a directory exists with the same name. You can use the `--output <file-path>` flag to provide an alternative name.
```

Despite explicitly using the `-o out.bin` argument, Deno:

- Logs that it's compiling "to foo"
- Attempts to emit the binary as `foo` rather than `out.bin`
- Fails if a `foo/` directory exists which should be irrelevant unless the `-o` was set to the same name

Additionally, if the compile command is run from any directory other than the project's direct parent like:

```bash
cd /tmp
deno compile ~/work/foo/main.ts -o out.bin
```

Deno still ignores the `-o` flag and instead emits a binary named `foo` directly into the current directory (i.e. `/tmp/foo`), not `out.bin`.

---

### Expected Behavior

- The compiler must respect the `--output` flag without referencing the source path or its parent directory.
- The output path specified via `-o` should always be used literally and without fallback logic.
- Compilation should succeed regardless of the current working directory or source location, as long as the `-o` path is valid and doesn't match any existing path.

---

### Additional Context

This appears to be a long-standing issue. A similar issue was previously raised in [#12759](https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/12759) but closed without being resolved, it only suggests using `--output` which appears to be broken as I stated above.

This bug creates serious friction in CI scripts, project automation, and build tools that rely on predictable output behavior.

title: How to scale OTEL instrumentation in Deno without opinionated defaults?
body: Hi everyone, especially @lucacasonato I'm currently integrating OpenTelemetry (OTEL) in Deno and have a question regarding the current approach. From my perspective, I’m struggling to understand how this implementation is meant to scale in the long run. It seems that there are no opinionated defaults, leaving it entirely up to the developer to define and manage everything manually. When a trace is started, I can modify the name and add values globally on the middleware level. However, when Deno makes sub-requests within that trace, these do not automatically inherit meaningful names or status information—they remain undefined unless explicitly set by the developer. This makes me wonder how one is supposed to scale instrumentation properly—would I need to manually update every single sub-request span myself? Or is this actually the intended way to use OTEL in Deno? Personally, I think it would make sense to provide at least some opinionated defaults, such as setting the span name to something like METHOD /pathname. Since Deno already tracks sub-requests, why not also set the status and a reasonable default name automatically? These pieces of information should already be available, so it feels like an unnecessary burden to require developers to handle them manually. Since I’m a newbie when it comes to OTEL, I’d really appreciate some clarification. Thanks in advance! 😊

title: [feat] Make backend js ecosystem future better
body:
### Feature Request

Make backend js ecosystem future better.

### What changed?

Program language like `rust` and `zig`, leads to new backend js/ts runtime like `deno` and `bun`.

### What is the problem?

`npm` is awesome.

To use awesome `npm` package for **backend**, usually need `Node.js` core module.

But, currently, because three runtime not able to share same `Node.js` core module, when use `deno` or `bun` with `npm` packages, there are compatibility issues.

Because `Node.js` `deno` `bun` does not able to share same `Node.js` core module and spec and test, `deno` `bun` reinvent the not-fully-compact wheel individually, and not reinvent-once-use-forever.

### What maybe the solution?

`Node.js` `deno` `bun` all support `napi`.

- `deno` napi since [pull/13633](https://github.com/denoland/deno/pull/13633), stable at [v1.31](https://deno.com/blog/v1.31#stabilization-of-node-api)

- `bun` is also [implementing](https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/158) napi

<details>
  <summary markdown="span">Extra</summary>

I don't know if override core module is needed for solution. 

If it does, I guess `Node.js` loader and `deno` importmap should works.

</details>

### What is the feature request?

- Rewrite `Node.js` core module using `napi`

- Rewrite `Node.js` core module test using `javascript`, so `Node.js` `deno` `bun` `browserify-XXX` can share **SAME** test

- Publish `napi` version of `Node.js` core module to `npm`

- Maybe publish to `npm` under a new organization `@backend-javascript-core-module-standard-committee/http`

### Related

- https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/50195

body:

### Description

**Bug Summary**
When upgrading from Pydantic V1 to Pydantic V2, I encountered a breaking change in model_validator(mode="before").
The same code works perfectly in Pydantic V1, but fails in Pydantic V2 when using model_validate_json(), throwing validation errors due to missing required fields.

**To Reproduce**:
The following is workable v1 codes

```py
import pydantic.v1 as pydantic

class BaseFruit(pydantic.BaseModel):
    name: str

    @pydantic.root_validator(pre=True)
    @classmethod
    def extract_name(cls, data: dict) -> dict:
        assert len(data) == 1
        fruit_name, fruit_attributes = data.popitem()
        return {"name": fruit_name, **fruit_attributes}

class Banana(BaseFruit):
    quantity: int

class NestedFruitOrder(BaseFruit):
    fruits: list["FruitType"]

FruitType = Banana | NestedFruitOrder

class FruitOrder(pydantic.BaseModel):
    fruits: list[FruitType]

FruitOrder.update_forward_refs()
NestedFruitOrder.update_forward_refs()

order_json = '{"fruits": [{"Susan": {"fruits": [{"Nested": {"fruits": [{"Mike": {"quantity": 5}}]}}]}}]}'
order = FruitOrder.parse_raw(order_json)
print(order)

```

Note that `update_forward_refs` is deprecated in v2 and the alternative one seems to be `model_rebuild`, but none of them makes any difference.

title: Nested Validation Errors in Pydantic Models Do Not Propagate Properly
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

When creating nested Pydantic models, validation errors from an inner model are not fully propagated to the outer model in certain scenarios, especially when exceptions are re-raised or wrapped during outer model validation. This behavior makes it difficult to debug issues in complex model hierarchies.

In the example below, an InnerModel fails validation because a field does not meet its constraints. However, when this failure occurs during the validation of an OuterModel, the error message only reflects the outer validation failure, potentially obscuring the root cause.



### Example Code

```Python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError, validator

class InnerModel(BaseModel):
    age: int

    @validator("age")
    def check_age_must_be_positive(cls, value):
        if value <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Age must be positive")
        return value

class OuterModel(BaseModel):
    name: str

    @validator("name")
    def create_inner_model(cls, value):
        # Attempt to create the InnerModel with invalid data
        # Intentionally use a negative age to trigger an error
        InnerModel(age=-1)
        return value

if __name__ == "__main__":
    try:
        OuterModel(name="Testing")
    except ValidationError as e:
        print("----- Python Exception Output -----")
        print(e)            # Human-readable error
        print("----- JSON Error Output -----")
        print(e.json())     # JSON-formatted error
```

title: PostgresDsn required host - should be optional
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

There is assumption in the code that host is required parameter in PostgresDsn. 

I do think there a number of cases where you won't submit `host` as a parameter as it's not required in many PG drivers. In Google Cloud you can connect in Cloud Run and other environment via unix socket file never going via host network. Example: https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/python-docs-samples/blob/main/cloud-sql/postgres/sqlalchemy/connect_unix.py#L36-L37 
```python
        # postgresql+pg8000://<db_user>:<db_pass>@/<db_name>
        #                         ?unix_sock=<INSTANCE_UNIX_SOCKET>/.s.PGSQL.5432
        # Note: Some drivers require the `unix_sock` query parameter to use a different key.
        # For example, 'psycopg2' uses the path set to `host` in order to connect successfully.
        sqlalchemy.engine.url.URL.create(
            drivername="postgresql+pg8000",
            username=db_user,
            password=db_pass,
            database=db_name,
            query={"unix_sock": f"{unix_socket_path}/.s.PGSQL.5432"},
        ),
```
The URI part `postgresql+pg8000://<db_user>:<db_pass>@/<db_name>?unix_sock=<INSTANCE_UNIX_SOCKET>/.s.PGSQL.5432` doesn't have at all host and that is ok for a lot of drivers.

PostgresDsn.build(scheme="postgres")
```

    a: PostgresDsn

empty_host = Model(a='postgres://user:pass@/app?unix=/cloudsql/project:us-east1:server/.s.PGSQL.5432').a

title: 'Url' type casts left around when serializing model to a dictionary
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

When serializing a model using URLs back to a dictionary, provided the URLs are properly represented, and validated using any of the network URL types, `Url/AnyUrl/HttpUrl` are explicitly formatted as type casts to the serialized dictionary  (depending on the exact pydantic v2 release)  which makes it hard to deterministically compare data as plain dictionaries in unit tests.
I used the word "deterministically" because prior pydantic  2.10.2 it seems like all URL types where formatted as `Url(<url>)`, but after **2.10.2** where there were adjustments to the URL validation constraints the actual types are honored in the serialized dictionary.
I don't think the type casts should be dumped to a serialized dictionary once a model has been successfully validated, making it completely transparent to the user what the model does/did in the background.

[1] https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/serialization/#modelmodel_dump

### Example Code

```Python
from typing import Optional
from pydantic import BaseModel, AnyUrl
from pprint import pprint


class SubModel(BaseModel):
    bar: AnyUrl
    baz: int = 1


class MainModel(BaseModel):
    foo: Optional[str] = None
    submodels: list[SubModel] = []


m = {
    "foo": "foo",
    "submodels":
        [
            {"bar": "https://example.com"},
            {"bar": "http://www.example.com/path", "baz": 2}
        ],
}

pprint(MainModel.model_validate(m).model_dump())


>>> python3 test.py
{'foo': 'foo',
 'submodels': [{'bar': AnyUrl('https://example.com/'), 'baz': 1},

title: Avoid Models Field Caching
body:
The TestModel does not refresh the `ModelStack` instance whenever the `current_model` changes. As a result, the `TestModel` fails to validate input data correctly when `current_model` is dynamically updated. Specifically, updating `current_model` from `Model` to `Model2` should allow the `TestModel` to use `Model2` for validation, but it continues to reference `Model1`.

**Code to reproduce:**
```python
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Model1(BaseModel):
    name: str

class Model2(BaseModel):
    numbers: list[int]

current_model = Model1

class ModelStack:
    def __getattr__(self, item):
        return getattr(current_model, item)

class TestModel(BaseModel):
    submodel: ModelStack()

print(TestModel.model_validate({"submodel": {"name": "John Doe"}}))  # Expected: submodel=Model1(name='John Doe')

current_model = Model2
print(TestModel.model_validate({"submodel": {"numbers": [1, 2, 3]}}))  # Expected: submodel=Model2(numbers=[1, 2, 3])
# Actual output:
# 
# pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 1 validation error for TestModel
# submodel.name
#   Field required [type=missing, input_value={'numbers': [1, 2, 3]}, input_type=dict]
#     For further information visit https://errors.pydantic.dev/2.9/v/missing
```

**Expected Behavior:** The `TestModel` should refresh its `ModelStack` submodel whenever `current_model` is updated. Therefore, after updating `current_model` to `Model2`, `TestModel` should recognize it and validate `{"submodel": {"numbers": [1, 2, 3]}}` correctly.

**Actual Behavior:** The `TestModel` does not refresh the submodel and continues to expect the fields defined in `Model1`, resulting in a validation error.

**Environment (if needed):**

Pydantic: 2.9.2

We first noticed an issue where Union validation wasn't being applied to nested LangChain models in an expected way, calling the nested model's validator in a way that raised an AttributeError and stopped model creation entirely (simple fix to remove typing on ControlFlow repo is [here](https://github.com/PrefectHQ/ControlFlow/pull/376)). 

However, I created an MRE that demonstrates the behavior without any of our logic. The code is below. We create a BaseModel with a single `model` field that is a union of the ChatOpenAI and AzureChatOpenAI langchain models. In one BaseModel, the OpenAI model is listed first in the union; in the other, the Azure model is listed first. 

When you instantiate the BaseModels, whichever langchain model was listed first in the union can be loaded successfully; whichever one is listed second fails. 

Note that this is using default union logic; setting to `left_to_right` doesnt seem to make a difference.

title: `model_dump` dict stays attached to the model's references for custom classes
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

It appears that `model_dump` creates a 'shallow' dump of the model: if one of the model attributes is a custom class containing mutable data, then changing the data in a dump of the model will also change it in the original model.

This feels unexpected as one would expect a 'dump' to be a record (e.g. [core dump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Core_dump), or [database dump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Database_dump)) of the model at the time of the dump, and changing that record should not change the original model. I think that either `model_dump` should do 'deep' dumps by default to actually create a dictionary record (and `vars(model)` can be used for `shallow` dumps) or `model_dump` should have an optional `deep` parameter.

A current workaround for this is if you use `model.model_copy(deep=True).model_dump()`, then it works as expected.

### Example Code

```Python
from pydantic import BaseModel

class MyClass:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data

class Model(BaseModel, arbitrary_types_allowed=True):
    var: MyClass

m = Model(var=MyClass([1, 2, 3]))
md = m.model_dump()
md['var'].data.pop()

# will give a result of [1, 2], so 3 has been popped from the model as well

### Description

Hi ! Thanks a lot for Pydantic
There is a difference in the way `PrivateAttr` is treated between instance methods and class methods.
